Mr. Speaker, hon. members of the
house will be interested to know that tenders have been received for the construction of a navigation lock at the northern end of the Canso causeway now being constructed across the strait of Canso between Cape Breton island and the mainland. T. C. Gorman (Nova Scotia) Limited, one of nine firms which tendered, submitted a tender of $4,817,777 and this tender has been accepted. speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, March 11, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned at six o'clock last night I was discussing the fact that at the time of the 1950 railroad strike the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) was the only member of the C.C.F. who voted for the resumption of railway service and the ending of the strike. Apparently he was the only one who was interested in the welfare of the farmers of Saskatchewan whose crops were lying out in the open exposed to the weather. Possibly the moving factor in his voting for the resumption of railway service was the fact that his own crop was exposed to the weather. That was the situation with respect to the C.C.F. stand on the railway strike.
Recently we had a short debate on the effect of railway strikes, namely, an increase in freight rates. I gathered from the speeches of my friends in that debate that possibly they might be going back to Saskatchewan and telling the people there what a good job they had done for them with regard to freight rates, that they had suggested to the government that the 7 per cent increase should not be put into effect, and that the government should do something about the board's decision in that respect. Their position was very clear in 1950. At that time they said they wanted the settlement of the strike postponed in order to protect the bargaining rights of the union. I have nothing against that, but that was their opinion. They wanted to be sure that free bargaining rights were maintained. They wanted to have us wait in order to protect free bargaining rights rather than have the strike settled on any other terms.
The C.C.F. party moved an amendment to the amendment to the motion for second reading of the bill to end the strike. Their amendment to the amendment included a provision that a wage increase of greater than 4 cents an hour should be granted to the workers. They did not say how much greater. They did not care how much


greater. It also included the following provision:
The implementing of the forty-hour week for forty-eight hours' pay at a date earlier than September 1, 1951.
They did not care what date it was as long as it was prior to that date. As far as they were concerned it could be back in the days of King John. So far as the monetary provisions were concerned, they were in favour of any settlement as long as the amount was big enough. Then they turn around and get up in the house and complain because freight rates have been increased. That is their position on freight rates.
I would not mention that except for the fact that the stage was being set here the other day for them to be able to go back to Saskatchewan and say what a fine job they had done for the people with respect to freight rates. We have had previous experiences along that line. In the days when we were discussing the settlement of the five-year wheat agreement with the United Kingdom, our friends in the C.C.F. were going around Saskatchewan and taking bows for voting for a final payment of 25 cents a bushel under the agreement, which would have amounted to some $350 million. Finally the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) had to get up in the chamber and straighten out that matter. No such vote ever occurred in the house. In speaking about the question the hon. member for Maple Creek said that most of the C.C.F. members from Saskatchewan had not even been in the house to vote for the $65 million that was paid to the farmers. The only reason we got the $65 million was the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) realized that something was coming to the farmers of the west from Great Britain and that as the government had taken part in the deal they were morally affected by it. It was only the fact that the Prime Minister realized that, that caused him to bring in a government measure to pay the $65 million, and if the government had been defeated on it they would have been out of office.
That is the only reason the farmers got the $65 million, and that was pointed out by the hon. member for Maple Creek. Prior to his doing so-and we knew he was going to do it-the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Smith) came over and sat on this side of the house. He said to me, "I am coming over here so I can have a clear view of our C.C.F. friends from Saskatchewan." He said, "I think there is one bird over there who is going to rise and take wing." When the hon. member for

Maple Creek made the statement that the boys from Saskatchewan in the C.C.F. party had not even voted for the $65 million, we were sitting over here and, sure enough, when he made the statement I found that the hon. member for Moose Mountain was a great psychologist. He certainly knew what was going to happen.
The bird got up and started to fly. He rose and said that he had voted for the $65 million whereupon the hon. member for Moose Mountain got up and said that he had not voted for it and had not been in the house. This occasion, I might say, was known among Liberal members from Saskatchewan as "operation mallard". It was a shooting expedition and was properly arranged. Our friend took his seat, but being a man of valour he got up again and started to fly as it were on one wing. He said he thought he was in the house that night and he thought he had voted for the $65 million. Whereupon the hon. member for Moose Mountain immediately got up again and said he knew the hon. member had not done so and every member in the house knew he had not.
The nails were really put in the coffin by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), himself, because in stating that he had got up that evening and voted for the measure he, proved beyond doubt that he was certainly wrong. As everybody knows, the vote was taken in the afternoon, and he could not possibly have been here in the evening and have voted for it. So much for that, Mr. Speaker. They go back to Saskatchewan and try to make out that these things took place in a different light than actually was the case.
During my term here since 1949 there have been three occasions on which our friends opposite have got up and said that the country should have price control. They went into that matter very extensively but we did not get price control.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The C.C.F.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is correct. I did not mean to include the hon. member who has just spoken. But they have risen in the house and suggested that we have price control. We have got along fairly well without it and in the only place where it was put into effect, south of the border, it was a gigantic failure. We have got along very well by doing exactly the opposite to what the hon. members across the way have suggested. A Liberal government has been in office for the past eighteen years. The C.C.F. also came into the house eighteen years ago, and they have consistently said

Mr. Harrison that the government was wrong on every measure that has been brought before the house. I think there is some reason to believe that the government has been right. The fact of the matter is that we have done fairly well in the past eighteen years.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Despite the government.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me discuss for a moment what our friends are doing in Saskatchewan. There has recently come to my attention a letter

I might say it could be regarded as a pastoral letter to his flock-put out by a friend of theirs by the name of A. M. Nicholson who, I understand, was the former member of parliament in this house for Mackenzie. He said:
It is important that an agricultural province like Saskatchewan should have a larger number of C.C.F. members in parliament determined to fight for a larger share of the national income for agriculture.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, if they fight for that the same as they did for the $65 million, and the way they have done for freight rates, I would say to the house and to the people of Saskatchewan that maybe there is some reason why they should not be here.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They won't be here.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the debate on price controls the C.C.F. stand is very clear. There again, were they working for the farmers in Saskatchewan? Well, I will give you the stand of one of them. My hon. friend the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) was trying to get them to clarify their position with regard to wages. They wanted food controlled-and that was the main thing they wanted to control-but they did not want wages controlled. The only person who grows food is the farmer and when you suggest that food only be controlled you are suggesting that only the farmer be controlled. This is what the hon. member for Halifax had to say on Tuesday, February 13, 1951, at page 332 of Hansard:
I would say also to my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party that I think it would be well for them to outline pretty carefully the way in which they want the various opposing groups to interpret their subamendment, because the support of the Social Credit party has been offered to them on the distinct understanding that the C.C.F. subamendment means that wage controls must be part of the program;
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said:
"Wages are controlled already."
Well, so much for that. Their policy is clear anyway at that time. They are not working for the farmer and their whole interest is that food prices be controlled and
2864	HOUSE OF
. The Budget-Mr. Harrison that wages be left uncontrolled. Anybody knows that those things which the farmer has to buy of a manufactured nature have about 70 per cent of their price made up by wages. Actually the C.C.F. are advocating that the prices of goods which the farmer has to buy go uncontrolled while goods that the farmer has to sell should be controlled. That is the way they have been operating as far as helping the farmer is concerned, since I have been in this house.
Now, I would like to say a few words on the budget. The first thing I would like to note here is a remark made in the debate in the provincial house by Mr. Fines, in his economic review of the situation in Saskatchewan. He says that the federal government is allowing a shrinking of export markets. He says there is a shrinking of export markets. Well, what is the answer to that? What shrinkage have we had in our export markets? Eighteen years ago, in 1935, when the C.C.F. came into this house and when this federal government took power, we had a total trade of $1,288 million. This year, eighteen years later, and following a policy laid down by this government which is exactly opposite to that suggested by our friends across the way, we have a trade of $8,386 million or an increase not double, not triple, not quadruple, but seven times the trade we had back in 1935. As I say, that has been achieved by following proposals which are in exact opposition to those of our friends across the way.
Our foreign trade last year did not decrease, as our friend Mr. Fines says, but it went up $100 million with the United Kingdom, and it went up $200 million with Europe and Latin American countries. In the case of those latter countries it showed an increase of 25 per cent. On a per capita basis we are the greatest trading nation in the world. There is nobody who can touch us. The biggest trading nation in the world, without taking into consideration the population factor, is the United States; but on a population basis in 1951 each citizen of the United States had a stake in foreign trade of $168. In Canada, in the same year, each Canadian had a stake in our total foreign trade of $577-over three times the figure for the United States. That should be answer enough to the finance minister in Saskatchewan when he states we are losing our export markets. That has been achieved anyway by a Liberal federal government.

It had been my intention sir, to say that, before this budget came down, what this country needed was a good five-cent cigar. After the budget came down it still needed a good five-cent cigar. Outside of that I think the budget has taken care of everything. These small items, even though they are insignificant, when they affect people personally often appear more important than major items.
I know that there are some Irishmen on the other side, so I will conclude by reading a report appearing in a Dublin paper. It says:
How are such miracles performed?-
They are talking of our budget.
-the Dublin Daily Irish Independent asks today in commenting on Canadian budget reliefs announced last week.
The cynic will recall that a general election is due this year-

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-says the newspaper in an editorial. Others will point to the almost fantastic growth of Canadian wealth during and since the war.
There are more fundamental reasons. The government has steadily followed a policy of directing investment into strictly productive channels.
My friend from Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) will appreciate that.
It has refrained from widespread increases in its own expenditure. It has adjusted taxation on business-
That is also something for my friend from Moose Jaw.
-so that companies are encouraged to plow back their earnings.
I think my friend from Moose Jaw will plow back some of his earnings. Under this budget he stands to gain something in the neighbourhood of $4,000 or $5,000 this year. We will get it back from him, however, because he will start another hardware store and hire three or four clerks and, ultimately, our friend "Doug" Abbott will have more than he had before-and that is free enterprise.
The Dublin paper goes on:
Finally it has recognized that the taxpayer is better able to use his money than even the minister of finance. It is a sound budget.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I observe that in his concluding remarks the hon. gentleman who preceded me found it difficult to discover words adequate to

describe the budget. Particularly did he find it difficult to find words adequate to describe the way in which the budget has helped one section of the community but has failed altogether to help the others.
Although the hon. member found it difficult to coin a single word to describe the budget, he found no difficulty in recognizing the fact that this budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on February 19 is a budget designed to serve almost exclusively the interests of business.
The budget has been called a number of names ranging from the complimentary to the critical. Whatever may be said about it, Mr. Speaker, whatever name may be applied to it-I have an idea of my own what it should be called-it is a fact that must be recognized by all that it is a business budget. It is a budget designed to help business, and it is good for business. The trouble with it is that the concessions to business are so great that there is no room for real concessions to be made to the average taxpayer. Whether or not one criticizes the help that has been given to business, it is I think a pity that the Minister of Finance attempted to dress his budget up and present it in the guise of a budget which would bring real relief to the average taxpayer, because it does no such thing.
The Minister of Finance coined his own name for the budget. He called it a social dividend budget. If he was going to give a dividend, as he said he was, to the Canadian taxpayer who has earned this dividend through his hard work, the sweat of his brow and his increased productivity, why did the minister not give the dividend to the average Canadian who has earned it instead of confining the real dividend to the man with invested income and to corporations themselves? We have had figures-I am not going to rehearse the record again-showing that the actual relief given to the average taxpayer, the man in the average income group between $2,400 and $3,000 a year, amounts to perhaps $1 this year or in some cases even a slight increase over what he paid last year. So, the man who earned this social dividend, who made it possible for the minister to give this dividend, does not get anything by way of a dividend. The substantial benefit is confined exclusively to the well-to-do, those who have substantial income from investments in corporations, and, as I have said, to the corporations themselves.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that instead of being called "the social dividend budget" it should be called "the social register budget", because the benefits are confined almost exclusively to those in the upper brackets who may find their names on the social
The Budget-Mr. Fulton registers of our larger towns and corporations. The budget gives nothing to the farmer or to the average Canadian. I think of the situation facing the ranchers in my constituency, with rising costs and declining prices for the things that they produce. There is no hope of tax reductions which amount to anything for them. Indeed, they are going to have to pay some sort of extra tax on the tires for their farm vehicles. If the minister had not confined his tax reductions, small as they are, almost exclusively to business, he would have been able to give some concessions to these hard-working Canadians. But no, the minister confined his concessions to those in the social register group, and the ranchers in my constituency will get little or nothing.
The minister had no concessions left over to make to the war veterans who are in receipt of war veterans allowance. They are still subject to that most miserable of institutions, that most discriminating principle called the means test. This test is still applied, with all its rigour, to the payment of war veterans allowance. I still hope the minister will find it possible, before the resolutions based on the budget are adopted, to make some change in that regard.
The minister has done nothing to help the average Canadian-as he might have if he had not confined his concessions to business- by way of reduction of the sales tax which so directly increases the costs of the things the average Canadian has to buy. And yet the budget had done nothing to leave him with a bigger share of his own income with which to meet these increased costs.
The minister says he is going to help the average Canadian. Why did he not reduce the sales tax on such non-luxury commodities as automobiles? The government likes to say that the sales tax applies to items which do not enter into the cost of living; that it is not a tax on necessities. Figures have been given by those in the automobile industry itself to show that the ownership of a car is not a luxury. The ownership of a car is not something confined to the rich people. The ordinary man who has to drive to work, the farmer who has to get from his farm into town, and the average Canadian generally, needs an automobile just as much as those who are in the social register group and who are helped by this social register budget. Those who need an automobile are not helped; they have not had the sales tax reduced.
Here is a statement made by the president of the Studebaker Corporation, as reported in the Toronto Star of February 9, 1953. This will give you an idea of the effect of this sales tax. He points out that in 1951
2866	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fulton the Canadian automobile industry produced
415,000	units with a sales value of $650 million. He pointed out that 81 per cent of the Canadian cars are owned by people earning less than $4,000 a year. He shows what happens in Canada when a man buys a $1,836 car. He pointed out that the average list price of the three lower-priced four-door sedans was $1,836 in Canada-that is the factory price. What happens when a Canadian buys this car? He pays $326 to the federal government, while in the United States he pays $134. Mr. Gaskin concluded by saying:
We feel it is time the taxing authorities realized what they are doing to the essentials of life.
That is the whole criticism we have with regard to this sales tax. It hits those in the lower income groups so hard. They are hit when it comes to buying the necessities of life. Tax is mounted upon tax so that they get no relief from this budget with respect to the amount taken away from them by income tax, and the burden of meeting the cost of living is increased by what they have to pay through sales tax.
Then, not content with trying to dress this budget up and present it as a budget giving relief to all Canadians, the minister made a certain statement with respect to the effect of the budget which simply cannot be left unchallenged. As I said, I think it is a pity the minister did not present the budget for what it is, that is, a budget for business, instead of trying to disguise it as a budget for the average Canadian. In the course of clothing this budget in its misleading garments, the minister made this statement which is found on page 2135 of Hansard:
A year ago taxes were reduced by $146 million a year. This evening I have proposed further reductions totalling $361 million a year. This makes the very substantial total of $507 million of tax reduction in two years . . .
Mr. Speaker, there could not be a more misleading statement. It is significant that there could not be a statement more carefully worded if it had been designed to give an impression which is totally false. It could not have been better calculated to give that false impression. What are the facts? The minister says:
This makes the very substantial total of $507 million of tax reduction in two years . . .
It means no such thing. The minister himself, in the course of his budget speech last year, stated that his reduction amounted to $116 million for the fiscal year which is now concluding. In the course of his budget speech this year he told us that the tax reductions will amount to $237 million for the fiscal year about to commence. Those two figures indicate a total of $354 million


tax reductions in two years, not $507 million. The Canadian people would have been better served by the minister if they had been told the truth about this matter in simple language, namely that, far from having their taxes reduced by $507 million in those two years, they will have reductions totalling only $354 million. Mr. Speaker, the difference between $354 million, the actual figure, and $507 million, the figure used by the minister- and repeated by him on the radio in a speech, in which he used almost exactly the same words, to describe the effects of the budget, a speech designed to have its effect in this year which is an election year-is $153 million; and $153 million is too big an error to have been made accidentally by as well informed a person as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott).

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I know that it would be improper for me to say in this house that the minister intended to do that. I am placing the one set of figures beside the other, and the figures for these two years beside the words used by the minister, and I am suggesting that the facts should be drawn to the attention of the Canadian people. That is as far as I wish to go.
When the minister used those figures he also repeated in his radio speech that tax reductions had been given amounting to 11 per cent, or rather that there had been an 11 per cent reduction in income tax. Actually the reduction is not 11 per cent, even on the basis of the minister's figures, for this year. The reduction is a maximum of 51 per cent. He then went on in his radio speech to say that tax reductions amount to $1 million daily. It is true that in a full fiscal year they may amount to almost $1 million daily, but they certainly do not amount to that figure in this election year and they certainly do not amount to $1 million daily in the taxes paid by the ordinary taxpayer of Canada. They certainly do not help the average taxpayers to the extent of $1 million a day.
I should also point out that if there is any reduction this year from the excessive rate applied in the past years, it is only made possible because those rates have been jacked up to a point so high that they amount to plundering the pockets of the taxpayers. If the rates are now reduced, by infinitesimal proportions so far as the average taxpayer is concerned, I suggest that he has no reason to be thankful to the minister because the minister now restores to the taxpayer a mere fraction of what belonged to him but which had previously been taken away from him.
Then of course the most significant feature of the budget is the fact that not one cent of tax reduction is brought about as a result of any economy being practised by this government. This year they are spending, according to the figures tabled in the main estimates, $314 million more than they have ever spent before, even although defence costs this year have not gone up in comparison to those of last year. The minister's constant theme is that increases in government spending are due to the mounting costs
The Budget-Mr. Fulton of defence. This year, according to the estimates, the costs of defence are within $1 million of what they were last year; yet government spending is going up by $314 million.
The minister's constant theme, repeated in every budget that he has presented here for the last three years, is that no further economies are possible; that the government is bending every effort to bring about economy in governmental services so as to prevent their costs from rising and that everything possible is being done. In fact, he challenged us-I recall that in the budget debate of 1950, when I was discussing this matter in the course of my speech on the budget, the minister indicated that he was prepared to challenge us to show where economies could be effected. Mr. Speaker, other members have shown, as I have-and as I intend to show this afternoon-examples of gross extravagance. These examples have been brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance and of the government but they ignore them. They simply repeat the same old theme that economies are impossible.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) adopts the same defeatist attitude. He says that there may be some "imaginary overtaxation" but that, because of the mounting costs of national defence, it is not possible to make any real reductions. Nothing could prove more clearly that we shall not get tax reduction until we get reduction in spending and that we shall not get reduction in spending until we get a change in government. I suggest to this government that if only the ministers and the government as a whole would display, in controlling government expenditure, one-quarter of the energy they display in saying that it is not possible to control it, we would get some results.
The Prime Minister calls it "imaginary overtaxation". The Minister of Finance says, "We have defeated inflation" and "We have cut government spending to the minimum". I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that a comparison of the rate by which government costs have mounted with the rate of increase in the consumer price index-which is about the nearest comparison one can get-suggests that the government have been falling far short of their duty in economizing in spending the people's money. I do not suggest that this is a perfect comparison by any means, but I have here some tables which I hope the house will permit me to put on Hansard. I will give an outline of them and if it is desired that I should read them in full, I can do so; they are not very long. I took the set of figures for government spending from the minister's own white paper tabled with the budget. I got the other set

When you compare the increase in government spending for the last five years, and deduct from the total figure of government spending the cost of defence, and of defence production, so that you are dealing only with non-defence spending, you find that since the fiscal year 1948-49 the amount spent by the government has gone up by 25-2 per cent. That is, there has been a 25-2 per cent increase, quite apart from what was spent on defence. On the other hand, the consumer price index in that same period has gone up by only 17-6 points, the index being based on the year 1949 as 100.
I should like to place these figures on Hansard. During the fiscal year 1948-1949, the average of the consumer price index for that 12-month period was 98-4. For the twelve months ended March 31, 1953, the average was 116, or an increase of 17-6 points. On the other hand the total government spending for the fiscal year 1948-49, apart from defence, was $1,907 million. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953, they spent $2,388 million, or an increase of 25-2 per cent, as against an increase in the consumer price index of 17'6 points.
With the consent of the house I should like to place these tables on Hansard.

speechtext:
I have given the gist of those figures. I have not time now to read them all into the record. If the hon. gentleman objects, I shall withdraw the table from Hansard, and shall not table it. I have given the effect of the figures, both the starting and ending points, with the over-all percentages. I believe I have given sufficient information so that hon. members may be able to make a fair comparison-a comparison which, Obviously, is so worrying to hon. members opposite that apparently they do not want the whole table to go on Hansard. So I am happy to leave the matter where it is.
The Minister of Finance has challenged us from time to time to show where economies can be made. In this connection let me give some figures of government spending. Recent figures tabled in the house show that there is to be spent an estimated total of $2,267,040.45 to provide Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation with a central office. Any hon. member who has driven down the Montreal road and has seen that palace will ask himself the question which I know the Canadian people are going to ask themselves: Do we vote these moneys for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to build houses for the Canadian people, or to build palaces for their head.office? They will ask this question: Do we vote money so that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation can build houses for the Canadian people, or so that it can build an auditorium in their head office at an estimated cost of $40,000, of which sum $2,500 was required as an extra to put in a spring-filled floor on which they can dance?
Then, I think the people of Canada will ask themselves why Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation required 281-5 acres for their head office, and why the buildings and grounds are going to take 21-3 acres out of that total of 281-5, which incidentally were purchased at an average price of $824.30 an acre.
And I think the Canadian people will ask themselves some questions about the proposed national film board building. The national film board is an organization of which I think the people of Canada may be proud, so far as most of the work of that organization is concerned. But I question very much whether the people of this country would be prepared to consent to the spending of $5,225,000 to build a central office for the film board in Montreal. I wonder if it would not be possible to establish an adequate central office without spending nearly five and a quarter million dollars?
I have been interested to look up comparative real estate prices in Montreal. Of course an absolute comparison is difficult to achieve.
The Budget-Mr. Fulton Figures I received in a return the other day show that this building is intended to provide 271,711 square feet of accommodation. We realize that the question of the locality must be taken into consideration. However, I have made some comparisons, and I have found that a building with 65,000 square feet in a comparable area in Montreal is for sale at the moment for $170,000. If one multiplies
65.000	square feet by four one obtains almost the equivalent of 270,000 square feet. If you multiply $170,000 by four you get $680,000.
Then take another example, a building west of Guy street in Montreal. This is a 2-storey, semibasement, reinforced concrete building, 55,000 square feet and priced at $225,000. There is another building with
130.000	square feet, 4-storey, reinforced concrete, sprinklered, for $500,000. Multiply
130.000	by two and you get 260,000 square feet; multiply $500,000 by two and you get $1 million.
Of course the comparison is not complete because these would not be new buildings. They would require alterations. I do not know whether it would be correct to say that if you could get a 130,000 square-foot building for $500,000 you could get one twice as big for only twice the price. I believe the cost of building per square foot comes down as the area goes up. But the difference between $1 million and $5,225,000 is $4,225,000. I suggest that you could do a lot of modification and alteration and modernization for $4 million, that is if you were not this government spending money. I wonder if they have looked into the possibility of acquiring one or more of these buildings and altering and modernizing them to suit their purposes with the object of saving some money. However, the possibility of saving money does not usually occur to this government. They just draw up their plans and decide to spend $5,225,000 of the people's money to provide a head office in Montreal for the national film board, without regard to cost.
There are many other examples of extravagance that could be cited, but I want now to turn to another matter, the difficulty of obtaining accurate information upon which to base suggestions for economy. We have had example after example where we have tried to get information and have been refused. We are asked to give concrete suggestions as to economies. I have given some. I want to point out to the house and to the country the difficulty of making concrete suggestions as to economies when information of extravagance is denied to us.
We have seen recent examples in the house this year, which, coupled with examples of former years, set a consistent pattern of

The Budget-Mr. Fulton the government refusing information because they know that information is going to embarrass them. We can see how absurd the situation has become when we remember that not so long ago the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) rose in the house and gave us a lecture on the desirability of obtaining information, of coming to the department and to the house to get information before making any statements. That same minister without a shadow of justification yesterday refused a motion for papers which would have given us information.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a question of privilege, the statement has been made by the hon. member that the Associate Minister of National Defence refused to give this information. That statement is not correct and is without a shadow of justification. The decision was made by this house and it was not a refusal by the minister at all.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will accept the correction made by the hon. member.. The refusal was made by the vote of the Liberal majority in this house; the Liberal majority backed up the minister who had said that he did not want to produce the information. That was enough for the Liberal majority in this house, just as it has been in the different committees of this house ever since I have been here. We have seen that pattern repeated time after time. Their majority supports the government in refusing to give us information because they know its production would be extremely embarrassing.
I am not going to repeat the request I made yesterday for the production of information, but I think we can all see why the government did not want that information produced. They knew that to do so would embarrass them. But in this instance a certain amount of that information fortunately has come into the hands of the public. These reports to which reference has been made, and copies of which I have been seeking to obtain for some time, deal with various activities of the Department of National Defence, and one of them particularly confirms the fact that everything said by Mr. Currie in his report is one hundred per cent correct. Furthermore, they show that the situation found by Mr. Currie was not a new situation but was one which had existed


for at least two years previous and was one of which the government had had knowledge.
The report describes a situation which existed two and a half years before Mr. Currie made his report, yet they did nothing about it. The situation was exactly the same when Mr. Currie came to make his inquiry, as is shown by a significant passage in the Currie report referring to the situation at Halifax. He points to that case as an example of what can be done to remedy conditions quickly. He says that when he first went to Halifax in September he found an appalling situation that was immediately drawn to the attention of the government, and when he went back in November he found that remarkable changes had been made.
The earlier report made in 1949 to the government-two years earlier-drew attention to the same situation in Halifax in the following words:
The slowness of the tradesmen (at Halifax) is a standing joke in the garrison. As an example I was shown a plywood partition about six feet wide and told that it actually took four carpenters two weeks to build it.
Another example:
I came to the conclusion that No. 6 works company must be known in Halifax by workmen as a good place to get a soft job and a- good place for third-class tradesmen to roost to their heart's content.
It would not be important by itself if information of this type were refused merely to a group of individuals, instead of to the House of Commons. We members are not entitled to preferential treatment as individuals, but we represent the Canadian public and in asking for information we do so as representatives of the people. We are asking for information to which the people are entitled.
We are asking for information where we think the people's money has been wasted so that we can make concrete suggestions in order that money may be saved and the people can have their taxes reduced. But when we find that the government is refusing information which would show the way in which the people's money has been wasted, that is important, not because the information has been refused to a member of the house but because it has been refused to the public. That is a matter which I believe will exercise the public and for which they will hold this government to account.
Now we find there was this report, based on a survey of army works services establishments made in 1949, two and a half years before Mr. Currie made his report, and it contains the following findings:
". . . the engineers (R.C.E.) are engaged in some very large (construction) projects and I think it

is fair to say that their attitude toward costs of construction indicates their attitude to finance generally, including money spent on staff. It seems to me that they are under the impression that . . . cost is no object when they want to do something.
Then the report refers to what took place at Shilo, and I point out to you, sir, that all this is on all fours with the remarks made by Mr. Currie two and a half years later when he complained about the war psychology and said that what we need is to get rid of war psychology, which counts nothing of cost, and set up an organization capable of functioning smoothly and of being integrated into our whole economy. These same findings were made two and a half years before. The situation was known to the government but they permitted the mess to continue. They permitted the waste of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of dollars of the people's money because to produce the information would have been embarrassing and because they did not know how or were unwilling to act upon the information themselves.
I do not know whether the report ever got to the department. Maybe it did not. If it did not, it should have, and if it did not I suggest the reason it did not was that the government did not like this report, it did not think too much of it, and therefore it thought it would put it away in a pigeonhole and not act on it. They might have got away with it and perhaps people would not have thought very much about it if it had not been for the fact that two and a half years later Mr. Currie came along and things became so bad they could not hide them any longer. They had to appoint an investigator and announce it. Mr. Currie was appointed and he found exactly the same thing as this report had drawn attention to two and a half years earlier.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

This afternoon I intend to refer to the budget only in general terms because it seems to me that in this long debate the details of the budget have been pretty well tossed back and forth from both sides of the house. I think the Canadian people have a pretty good idea of what is in it and how everybody feels about it.
It seems to me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has displayed great ingenuity and resourcefulness in spreading the tax concessions he has made throughout such a large segment of the Canadian economy. I, personally, am very pleased to see that he was able to eliminate the nuisance taxes and also I am pleased to see the fine job that he did in encouraging investment of Canadian people's savings in Canadian industry.
I think it is a matter of great gratification to us all that our per capita debt continues to be reduced and that our net debt is a smaller proportion of our national productive capacity than it has ever been. Despite the last great war and our great contributions to it, and the gifts which this country has made since, we have the second highest standard of living of any people on earth. I think that is a great thing to realize. When we actually consider the per capita debt that we owe, and the future of this country, we can probably say that Canadians are the richest people in the world.
I would say that we should in all fairness give a certain measure of credit to this government for the prestige this country holds throughout the western world. I am sure that when Canadians go overseas to attend the coronation this year they will be able, and I quote the words of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), "to say with meaning and to say with pride that they are Canadians".
This has, of course, been called an election budget. Perhaps it is more fair to say that this is the last budget we shall have before *an election.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just civic taxes. I think perhaps the attitude of British Columbia towards the federal government is partly psychological. We are hemmed off from the rest of Canada by those great ranges of the Rocky mountains. I find that there is a lot of merit in what the late Senator G. G. McGeer said when he was in this house. He said that it was 3,000 miles from Vancouver to Ottawa but it was 10,000 miles from Ottawa to Vancouver. I find that people out there still think that way, and perhaps that is why they are not as familiar with the workings of the federal government as are the people of some of the other provinces.
I think it might be of some value to look at the picture in British Columbia and see just what the similarity is between the position this federal government holds there and the position that the last Liberal government held there before they were thrown out. Both this government and the last Liberal government we had out there were administering the affairs of the country at a time of great general prosperity. Great general progress was being made. I think the same thing, of course, can be said of this government here. The government in British Columbia was honest, and I think we can concede this one is; and, in the main, the governments were both efficient. There is a certain attribute of all governments, I think, after they have been in power for a long time, that they sometimes give the appearance that they feel they are infallible and that they have ineffable wisdom. The people of British Columbia feel, and this has been expressed by a number of members from British Columbia, that this government has not done too well as far as the control of radio and television is concerned. They feel,
I think, that for a free enterprise government it is not right that we should have the industry controlled by a government agency; they feel that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should not be both judge and jury.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has taken you seven long years to find these things out.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I am a little slower on the pick-up than my hon. friend but I often try to be more objective-after all, I am an Independent.
When I am speaking of this government control of radio and television, which is essen-


tially, as it should be, a private industry in this country, I think it might be well if the government just gave some consideration to the thought that it would not be a bad thing for the country if Canadian Pacific Air Lines were allowed permission by the air transport board to put another competing air cargo service through. I think perhaps a little competition for Trans-Canada Air Lines might be an excellent thing.
There is another matter that Liberal members and members from all sides have mentioned, but I expect the government listens to the Liberal members more than the others. I heard the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall), the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), and numerous other British Columbia Liberals ask the government if it would not set up the veterans affairs committee and just take a look at the problem facing old war veterans. Perhaps there is something we can do for them.
In British Columbia I think we have the greatest percentage of people on war veterans allowance, and the people of British Columbia say that they hear that old folks are not getting along very well in some instances. Perhaps we should set up this committee and take a look at the whole picture, to satisfy the people of Canada generally that we are trying to take care of some of these problems that are arising in their lives.
It seems to me, too, that the people of British Columbia-and as I say they are a long way away-feel that this government has not explained too well or answered too clearly the charges of some of the members of the opposition here that there has been waste and extravagance in the administration of certain government departments. I think perhaps they are thinking of the Department of National Defence. I have often wondered why it would not be a good thing if perhaps the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), or perhaps all members of parliament, explained to the Canadian people that these so-called luxuries and amenities we have provided for the members of our armed services are really the result of the fact that we have voluntary military service in this country. I think it is generally agreed by most Canadians that voluntary military service is what we want, except in time of war. If that is what the Canadian people want, then we must recognize that our armed forces in peacetime are servants of the Canadian people as are members of parliament. If we are going to attract these people to our armed services, then we must compete, in both wages and the

amenities of life, with the very high standard of civilian living which obtains throughout Canada now.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And assure them that they will have a living after they are through fighting.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I imagine we are doing a fairly good job on that. I think we all agree that, so far as pensions for members of the armed services are concerned, we must all recognize that they cost money. When we are quoting comparable figures concerning what it costs to maintain a man in this country as compared with what it costs in a European army, we are not being fair because the European armies do not have a voluntary system of military service.
Those are all the general remarks I am going to make concerning the budget. I come now to a problem that is really vital to my riding, perhaps more important to my riding than it is to any other riding in British Columbia. As hon. members know, lumbering and fishing are the two great stand-bys of the economy of Comox-Alberni. Last fall during the debate on the speech from the throne I referred to the fishing industry. From what I have read in the press concerning a speech delivered by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) to the fishermen's union in Vancouver recently, I have great hopes that we may be able to do something for that industry with regard to trade with the United Kingdom.
I want to talk today-I am very glad to see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has come into the house-about the logging industry, which is one of the basic industries in the economy of British Columbia and particularly my riding. As the minister is aware, our new Social Credit government in British Columbia has applied a new 10 per cent tax on logging profits. This action, of course, is particularly unfair to the principal industry in my riding. I do not want it to be inferred that I am placing the entire blame for this action on the Social Credit government. It seems to me that it is a fact that for the past ten years, since our tax agreements have been in effect, the federal government has taken unfairly tens of millions of dollars out of the B.C. logging industry, and has been putting practically nothing back into the forests of British Columbia. I say "unfairly" because timber cutting by owners out there, both large and small, has been subjected to a virtual capital gains tax imposed by this federal government. This one industry has been singled out from all industries in Canada for a capital tax of approximately 50 per cent, by reason of the methods of computing timber values for income tax purposes.
The Budget-Mr. Gibson In the past ten years the federal government has taken at least $40 million, I say unjustly, from the British Columbia timber owners, both large and small, and to that industry there has been very little contribution from the federal exchequer. When I think of what this government does for the prairie provinces, with the P.F.R.A. and the P.F.A.A.; the bonus of $65 million to wheat producers, and then another $40 million this year to support hog and beef prices, it seems to me that for the tremendous revenue the minister has been taking out of British Columbia he has not been putting very much back. Usually, you know, if anyone in Canada "clips" the Minister of Finance for $2 million, he is up here screaming like a wounded steer. In this particular instance when he read about this new tax in the newspapers he realized that he was going to lose half of it, but for some reason or other I have not heard him say anything about it as yet. He took it very calmly.
The same thing, of course, applies to the mining industry in British Columbia. It seems so incongruous that this parliament should be asked to vote gold mining assistance, and then allow the provincial government to take that money back from the mines. Perhaps it would be better to give the money direct to the provincial government. The Minister of Finance has had such good plucking from this goose for so long that the logging industry is really his golden goose. He has this special taxation on the industry's capital gains, and it would seem to me he would have had some measure of consideration for that industry. Instead of that, under the dominion-provincial tax rental agreements, he takes the best provider he has and stakes him out for tiger bait. It is quite obvious that if the minister writes into an agreement that he does not want the province to tax anyone else except loggers and miners, the ministers of finance in the provinces are going to take a crack at them as soon as they need money.
Perhaps we cannot blame the minister of finance in British Columbia for having done this. As I say, the federal minister has protected all the other industries in Canada except these two industries which have been afforded no protection at all. I feel that the minister should take a look at these taxation agreements to see if they are actually fair. One must realize that in British Columbia 40 per cent of the tax revenue which comes to the minister is based on the timber industry. It seems to me that if we extract more from a province like British Columbia, which has an extractive economy, it would be fairer if the minister, in his taxation agreements with all the provinces, would

The Budget-Mr. Gibson insist that the provinces not tax mining or logging any more than the provinces tax anyone else. He might say, if you cut five billion feet of timber in British Columbia, perhaps I will allow you fifty cents or a dollar a thousand. That would be a much fairer basis of working. The same principle should be applied as was applied in the prairie provinces, where we have an extractive industry in that they are probably depleting their soil, and where this government has taken very effective steps to see that money and effort were put back into maintaining those assets. Actually, we are taking care of their extraction.
It is a particularly difficult thing for the small loggers in British Columbia. The federal government has been taking all this revenue from the forests of British Columbia and, as a result, the provincial government has not been able to make the forests pay. This has resulted in the government having to charge a far too high stumpage to the small loggers. The old companies that went in forty or fifty years ago got timber as cheap as twenty-five cents a thousand. Some of that timber is standing right alongside timber for which the present provincial government is asking small loggers to pay $20. It does not take much imagination to see how difficult it is for the small man on that basis. The provincial government feels, and with some justification, that the timber sold thirty or forty or fifty years ago was sold in a very poor deal. However, instead of putting on another tax, it seems to me the provincial government should come to Ottawa and try to get our present Minister of Finance to disgorge some of these, I would say, almost ill-gotten gains acquired over the past ten years.
Perhaps I appear to be speaking with some bitterness this afternoon, Mr. Speaker. Of course, I was brought up in this district of Comox-Alberni. My friends and their families have been pioneers there and brought it to its present stage of development. When I look over that beautiful land, partly stripped of the wonderful forest wealth that we had there; when I think that a large measure of the wealth has come down here to enrich the coffers of the federal treasury; and when I see so many people in my riding isolated, with no road transportation, and this government refuses to connect up our airports there with military roads-we have two magnificent airports at Port Hardy and Tofi.no on Vancouver island-I can understand why some folks out there have a certain amount of bitterness as far as the general taxing powers of this country are concerned.


Sometimes I have heard some of them say it is a bad deal ifi that we ever went into confederation.
Vancouver island is a natural protective barrier for half the British Columbia coast. Yet our Department of National Defence has not seen fit to put in any highway communication to those airports that I have mentioned. If those two airports were ever taken over by hostile forces, they would certainly be able to be a great menace to the whole of the Pacific northwest. I have often wondered whether this Department of National Defence rather feels that we are, as it were, expendable in that country out there. I certainly cannot imagine any members from the maritimes in this house putting up with a similar condition. Can you imagine the people in Nova Scotia not having roads along their coast, for national defence if for nothing else? As I say, the Pacific coast is much more vulnerable to attack than is the Atlantic coast.
I know that the Minister of Finance is anxious to take part in the debate this afternoon, so I do not intend to speak much longer; but I just want to say this. As far as British Columbia is concerned, and the timber industry out there, I feel that we are getting a rather shabby deal from the federal government here. I sincerely hope that the Minister of Finance and the government will at least think over what I have told them today.
Just before I pass on, I should like to say another thing in support of what the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) said the other night with regard to river bank protection in British Columbia along that vital avenue of communication for both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. I certainly hope that my good friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) will do something in behalf of the hon. member for Fraser Valley and will see if he cannot protect our national lines of railway by river bank protection in the Fraser valley.
I am sorry that the leader of the Social Credit party is not in the house because I thought perhaps I would give him a little bit of advice this afternoon, if I might be so presumptuous as to do so. It just seems to me that hon. members should take a little bit more care down in that corner of the house because, from what I have heard in this debate, it seems to me that some of his henchmen down there have been consorting too closely with the members of the C.C.F. party. Some of them appear to be almost becoming socialists. I think we should ask you, Mr. Speaker, to put up an iron curtain between the two parties.

I listened with great interest the other night to the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Thomas) when he was speaking. It seems to me that this young man needs a lesson in elementary economics. I do not think that his leader should try to teach him social credit economics because I do not think he would understand those. I do not think even the Minister of Finance understands them. But I think his leader ought to give him an education in just basic economics.
The hon. member for Wetaskiwin the other night was speaking of the surpluses that corporations in Canada had created in the last twelve years. He computed them roughly at about $6 billion; and if I recall correctly what he said, he suggested that the Minister of Finance should make a capital levy on that $6 billion. It seemed to him that there was too much money drifting around loose some place, and he thought it was an excellent plan to put a capital levy of one-eleventh on that amount. I do not think that the hon. member realizes, of course, that this procedure was more or less tried out in the old country by the socialists there but they found that it did not work very well.
I might also point out to him-I will just give him an elementary lesson in economics- that surpluses of this kind of course are usually invested in brick, mortar and in the creation of jobs for our Canadians. He says that corporation surpluses have increased by $6 billion in that time. I think it is a good thing that those surpluses have increased because we have almost one million more wage earners in Canada. If his arithmetic is sound he will realize that it takes $6 billion at least to create jobs for an extra million people. I can tell him something about the logging industry, for instance. When I was a young fellow, about thirty years ago, I used to go out in an Indian dug-out canoe. My brother and I were hand loggers. We would get a canoe for $20. We got a pump jack for $75. We had two saws for about $10 apiece. We had a peevy, an eight-pound sledge hammer and two five-pound felling wedges.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And elbow grease.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and a lot of ambition. Actually that is about all the capital you had to have at that time. But I would point out to him that, for one man to be employed in the logging business now, it takes a capital investment of $10,000. While our socialist friends and perhaps our friend the hon. member from Wetaskiwin may think it is an evil thing that it should take that much, I am still sure that they are extremely glad that the economy of Canada is such that we have been able to provide tools of that
The Budget-Mr. Abbott kind to create the efficient economy that we have which produces so much money and so much prosperity for the people of Canada.
I am sure the Social Credit leader is going to speak later in this budget debate. I hope that he will really assure us at that time that this capital levy that has been suggested is not a standard policy of the Social Credit party, because I think the people of British Columbia would be greatly interested to have that point made clear to them before the next provincial election. It seems to me that perhaps Alberta and British Columbia are hardy enough to stand a period of Social Credit provincial government, but I shudder to think what would happen to the financial standing and the prestige of this country if the Social Credit party ever took over our federal government and obtained control of our banking and currency. I am afraid that we would all agree that such an eventuality could have nothing but disastrous results.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not ordinarily take part in the debate again at this time on the subamendment moved by my friend the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). However, it will not be possible for me to be here in the house tomorrow. This debate has gone on for some time-I hope it will not be unduly prolonged-and there are a few matters which have been raised in the course of the debate with which I should like to deal before it concludes. I do not intend to detain the house for long, but there are a few things that I want to take up.
I have listened carefully to most of the speeches that have been delivered on the budget; and those I have not been able to listen to I have read in Hansard. I followed closely the speech of the financial critic of the official opposition, and it seemed to me that he found it a bit difficult to make up his mind just what line he was going to take. At the outset he taxed me with producing an election budget. Then in the next breath he reproached me for having failed to give any relief to the majority of the voters. Then he seemed to approve the reduction in the corporation tax, but at the same time he argued that this relief should have gone somewhere else

I suppose to places where the voters are more numerous. All I can say is that I can only leave that criticism to the good judgment and the common sense of the majority of the voters themselves.
The hon. gentleman devoted most of his time to making a point that the tax cuts could have been greater if the government had been more prudent in its spending; and he indulged in the usual sweeping, general
2878	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Abbott charges of waste, extravagance and inefficiency without, as usual, particularizing any of those charges. The fact that he or others assert that to be the case does not make it so. I certainly would be the last to assert that in any spending program of four and one half to four and three quarters billions of dollars every cent was wisely spent, and that no errors of judgment had been made. That, of course, would be manifestly absurd.
But I do say this, that there has not been widespread waste, widespread inefficiency, widespread extravagance. And I do say this, that every effort has been made by government departments and by my own department to see that the taxpayer gets the maximum value for his dollar. And we will continue to exercise that care. Whether or not the results satisfy the people of Canada-I am sure, of course, that they will not satisfy the opposition-remains to be seen. I think they do; and I make this further assertion, that Canada is getting as good or better value for its defence dollar, and for its expenditures on public matters in other fields, as any other comparable country.
One or two members have been a bit more specific in their criticisms of alleged waste and extravagance. One was the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) who, I am sorry, is not in his seat at the moment. He read from what appeared to be a typewritten sheet excerpts from letters which he said he had received from taxpayers complaining about what they believed to be wasteful expenditure in connection with the construction of radar stations. That was dealt with in part the other day by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and dealt with, I thought, pretty effectively. My criticism of the method used by my hon. friend from Nanaimo is this, that in reply to a question which I put to him he acknowledged that that was the first time he had brought the matter forward; that he had not brought it to the attention of the Department of National Defence, or my department, and that he was bringing it forward in the house without any names, without places, without dates or anything else.
I am going to make this suggestion to him. He said he was concerned about the position of the taxpayers. So am I, as I assured him at that time. And I suggest to him that he could serve the taxpayer better if he had called a stenographer here in the House of Commons, who is paid by the taxpayer, and dictated a letter to be transcribed on paper, which is also paid for by the taxpayer, handed it to a messenger, who is also paid by the Canadian taxpayer, and sent it down to me or to some other minister, also paid by the Canadian taxpayer.


I have a highly competent staff who would have been happy to investigate a matter of that kind, and who would have done it. And then, if my hon. friend was not satisfied with the explanation, not only would he have been within his rights but it would have been his duty to bring it forward in the house. But he would not have got headlines in that way.

Another self-appointed guardian of the treasury is the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). He is not given to understatement, either, when it comes to setting forth what he conceives to be waste and extravagance in government expenditures. It is now fairly clear that the government has tossed money around recklessly on defence in the past year.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I do not think it is so reckless.
And then he went on to say this:
I charge this government with milking the Canadian taxpayer in those years to provide frills in defence spending.
I ask you to mark those words, "frills in defence spending". Then he proceeded to enumerate, presumably, what some of those frills are:
In the first place, as has been pointed out in recent days, you will find 25 contracts for landscaping various government buildings, with more than a million dollars spent for this particular service. At Fort Nelson, $27,500 was paid out for the construction of a single well. At Wainwright, Alberta, a swimming pool cost $22,000; a gymnasium, $280,000; bowling alleys, $54,000. Is it for such things that this government is taxing the Canadian people?
Well, my answer is yes. We are asking young Canadians to join our armed forces as a career, and if necessary to fight for their country. We hope they will not have to. If those young men were working in the hardware business in Moose Jaw-I am assuming there is a Y.M.C.A. in Moose Jaw-they could swim in the Y.M.C.A. building there. They could use the gymnasium. snrubs around it.
