Then my hon. friend from Moose Jaw went on to enumerate a lot of other things, and I shall not weary the house by reading them all. He said, for instance, that $25,000 was spent for air-conditioning the office of the central ordnance depot, that a ventilating system for a building had cost $48,000, and so on.
I shall not attempt to place on record all the statements he made. But he made no attempt to demonstrate that these prices were out of line with what they should have cost. They were all done by public tender, and the lowest tenders were accepted. I do not know whether there was any hardware in any of them, but if there was, and if it was provided by my hon. friend, I have no doubt the prices would have been a bit higher.
My point is that that sort of criticism could not be more superficial. It is absolutely meaningless, except to try to convince people, people who read only the headlines, that there is something wrong with the government spending program: "Charge of Waste and Extravagance; Young Member from Moose Jaw Lashes out at Government Waste". Well, so far as I am concerned, the public can draw their own conclusions. These charges of widespread waste and extravagance and inefficiency in my judgment neither exist nor have they been substantiated in the house by hon. members who have attempted to do so.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) delivered his usual sincere, consistent and thoroughly orthodox criticism of the budget, from his point of view. I have heard the hon. member make the same type of criticism of budgets for 13 years, and his 68108-183
The Budget-Mr. Abbott speech was no surprise to me. The hon. member is a convinced socialist; and he consistently pleads with me that when taxes are to be raised, the burden should be put on the rich, or the more well-to-do. And when taxes are to be lowered he would like to have most of the reduction given to those who are less well off. I concede that he is thoroughly consistent in arguing that inconsistent policy. I am sorry I cannot meet him in that respect, but I have gone about as far as one could go, with responsibility.
Let me review what has happened in connection with our taxation program. The house will recall that in 1949 we brought in a post-war scale of income tax rates, steeply progressive, which represented the lowest point reached at the end of the war, and was about half the rates of wartime taxation. It was the best and lowest scale we were able to devise at that time. Incidentally that was confirmed in September after the June election. In the budget in the spring of 1950 we made only minor tax reductions. Then came Korea, and in September of 1950 I brought in my budget and recommended almost a 15 per cent increase in the corporation tax. I increased the excise tax on a line of less essential goods from 10 to 15 per cent, but did not touch the personal income tax. That tax remained at the 1949 schedule.
Then in the spring budget of 1951 we imposed a 20 per cent surcharge on corporation taxes and personal income taxes. Mark you, that 20 per cent surcharge on the corporation income tax was on the rate increased by 15 per cent in September, 1950. At the same time we increased the special excise tax from 15 to 25 per cent on this list of less essential goods to which I have referred. That was the tax scale which prevailed through that year.
In the spring of last year, when it became evident and more clear as to what expenditures were likely to be in connection with the war in Korea and our brigade group in Germany and our defence forces by and large, we eliminated about one-third of the surtax on the personal income tax but made virtually no change in the corporation tax. That was 50-6 per cent and we eliminated the *6 per cent to round it off to the even 50 per cent. We dropped the special excise tax rate from 25 back to 15 per cent.
In this budget we are recommending the complete elimination of the surtax that remains on the personal income taxpayer and are putting that back to the 1949 level. Mark you, that was a level where the exemptions were higher and the tax rates lower., and substantially lower, than in any comparable country in the world.
2880	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Abbott
So far as the corporation tax rate is concerned, this year we are making very modest reductions in the standard rate of three percentage points. With respect to the smaller businesses it is true that the relief is much more substantial. We are not touching the special excise tax rate which remains at 15 per cent, or the general sales tax rate which has not been increased since 1935 except by the 2 per cent added to pay for old age security. So that in effect added defence costs so far as the tax structure is concerned are being borne by the corporation income taxpayers and the special excise taxes.
As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar pointed out the other day, I recognize that in large part the corporation tax will be passed on to the users of goods and services produced by the corporations so that to that extent the people are continuing to pay their share of defence costs through that medium. But that is the picture; that is the way in which tax reductions have been made.
As the house knows, I rarely quote from editorials or periodicals or publications, but I am going to depart from that rule today and quote from a recent issue of the Economist. I do not need to indicate the standing of this publication. It is one which the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell) often quotes. It is clearly not a Liberal party organ and it is not published in this country. Some hon. members may have seen the issue of February 21 which contains am extremely interesting series of articles entitled "Canada, The Expanding-Economy". This article indicates what has been taking place in this country during the last ten or fifteen years. I commend the reading of these articles to all hon. members who may be interested ini seeing an outside picture of what is going on in this country. I should like to quote just one short passage from one of the articles headed "Capital, Not Men" as follows:
The financial policies of the Canadian government have been commendably strict, and have generally kept inflationary forces well in hand. Indeed, it is one of the interesting paradoxes of the postwar years that the country which has been developing most quickly has had less inflation than almost any other. There could be no more convincing evidence of wise financial and political management.
My good friend the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), in one of his usually able speeches, yesterday quoted from a speech that I had made last December before the Canada Club in London. He also quoted with approval a portion of my budget speech in which I said that the very satisfactory results which we had had during the last year or two had been due in large
(Mr. Abbott.]

measure to the added efforts of the Canadian people. Then he quoted with some disapproval a further passage in which I said that these results had been due in part to wise political management. His thesis was that it would have happened anyway, that it was all due to the war and to other causes.
Of course that is a philosophy with which I do not agree. My friend is a socialist, and I respect his beliefs. I know perfectly well that the views which he voices are sincerely held by him and have been so held for a great many years. As he knows, I have a different political and economic philosophy.
In the last issue of the Economist which has come to my hand

this is the last time I am going to quote from that publication- there is a series of articles devoted to Australia. They contrast the development in Australia with the development in Canada, I must say to the advantage of Canada. As the house knows, for the greater part of the last ten or fifteen years Australia has been governed by a socialist government. I should like to quote briefly from this article in the Economist of March 7 entitled "Developing Dominions". After outlining the contrast between the development in Australia and in Canada it goes on to say:
This contrast between Canada and Australia has a broad significance. Is Canada's economic development more forceful and healthy simply because Canada has greater natural advantages- of resources, geography or climate? Or does the divergence in economic prospects reflect social and political differences that are to some extent within the control of governments?
Then after elaborating a bit, this is the way in which the question put in the first paragraph is answered:
The reason why Canada is taking the opportunity so well, and Australia so hesitantly, is political. It lies in economic policies, not in the facts of nature. This is not to say that change-a shift back to the expansion of primary production-is easy for Australia. The excessive concentration on secondary industry reflects inexorable social pressures that can hardly be overcome until the deep class and political tension among the nine million Australians has been reduced. There is, nevertheless, some comfort to be drawn from the comparison between Canada and Australia: for its lesson is that to some extent, at least, a country and its government can choose expansion or reject it.
While I would be the last to assert that the remarkable growth which has taken place in this country during the last ten or fifteen years has been due entirely to government policy-I have never said that-I do submit that it has been due to a combination of good people, good luck and good management, and I do say that good management has played a significant part. I for one am proud to have formed part of the government which has formulated and put into effect policies

which I think have contributed significantly to the outstanding results which have been achieved in this country during the last ten or fifteen years.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if I may digress for a moment, I should like to deal with a point made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) in the speech he delivered the other day. In the course of that speech he had something to say about the amount of income tax paid by farmers in the central provinces compared with the amount of tax paid by farmers in the west. He produced some figures which purported to show that the average Ontario farmer paid less tax than the average Saskatchewan farmer, although the Ontario farmer's net income was larger. Similarly other figures were given as proof that the average Quebec farmer paid less tax than the average British Columbia farmer, although the Quebec farmer's net income was higher.
I have not the slightest quarrel with my hon. friend's arithmetic, but I do object to his use of the figures which he produced. The use of averages can of course often be very helpful, as I hope to show, but it can also be very misleading; and although I am sure these figures which were produced by my hon. friend were not intended to be so-

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, no-the averages which he used were in fact misleading for this reason.

speechtext: You do not recognize a gentleman when you hear one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may be perfectly good arithmetic, Mr. Speaker, to say that an average income tax liability of $30.95 was incurred for 1950 by each of the 112,018 occupied farms in Saskatchewan, but it is at least as accurate, and much more meaningful, to say that 10,950 Saskatchewan farmers incurred an average tax liability of $316.62 and the remaining Saskatchewan farmers incurred none at all. Similarly the $12.60 liability for the 149,920 occupied farms in Ontario might in my opinion be better expressed as an average tax liability of $196.57 for 9,610 farmers.
This example illustrates what I had thought was the well-known fact that income tax is not calculated on the average income of a whole group in any locality but upon the actual income received by each individual taxpayer. No one can determine how much tax should be paid by a particular group except by ascertaining the net income of each individual in the group and applying those provisions of the Income Tax Act that 68108-183J
The Budget-Mr. Abbott are appropriate in each case such as the exemption for dependents and the total amount of tax so found for each individual. What it is important to know then, it seems to me, when comparing the tax potential of one group of individuals with another, is not the average net income but the number of individuals who have a taxable income and the way in which this income is distributed among the various income brackets.
Unfortunately there are no statistics available that show the distribution of farmers' net incomes by provinces. However, lack of statistics need not prevent us calling to mind certain well-established facts. First, farming operations in Saskatchewan are, I think it is fair to say, on the whole on a larger scale and more highly mechanized than in Ontario, and might be expected to yield a larger net return per farm. It is not surprising, therefore, that for 1950 there were slightly fewer farmer taxpayers in Ontario than in Saskatchewan and that the average tax paid was also somewhat smaller. Second, the average size of the farm family is much smaller in Saskatchewan than in Quebec, and somewhat smaller than in Ontario. This means that Saskatchewan farmers on the average have smaller exemptions and consequently larger taxable incomes than Quebec farmers even if their average net incomes are the same.
These are two averages which I submit are useful and not misleading. There are many other factors which have to be taken into account in making a proper comparison of potential income tax liability in the west and in the central provinces, but I hope I have said enough to indicate the danger of jumping to conclusions on the basis of insufficient evidence. I know that I speak for my colleague the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) as well as for myself when I say that every effort is being made to ensure that Canadians of all occupations and in all provinces are being given fair and equal treatment under the present income tax law.
The present budget which is before the house is based on the assumption that Canada will stay prosperous with a moderate expansion in production over the next twelve months. Prices and the cost of living appear to be relatively stable. Revenue estimates assume only a modest increase in the gross national product of 4 per cent. Prudent and reasonable estimates have been made regarding expenditures for the coming year, and on the basis of these careful, responsible calculations it appeared that about $250 million was available. More revenue would be coming than would be needed to meet expenditure and accordingly, in line with past policies

The Budget-Mr. Brooks during the last two or three years, this surplus was devoted to tax reduction.
The tax reduction proposed has, I sincerely believe, been fairly and sensibly distributed. There is nothing devious or misleading about the budget. It is not an election budget; it is not a rich man's budget. It is an honest and straightforward budget in which an earnest attempt has been made to pass on to the people of Canada, in as fair a manner as possible, the reward for an excellent record of hard work and production.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not expected to be placed in the difficult position of following the minister this afternoon. I have listened to his remarks with much interest, and I would say that his speech was very modest and mild compared with the budget speech he delivered a short time ago. I do not think anyone could claim that he dealt with the subject with the same assurance as he showed previously.
The budget debate is usually a wide-open one and allows great latitude of discussion by the members of the house. I intend to take advantage of this opportunity to dwell on some matters which concern my part of the country particularly. I think that is only right, because the budget itself affects the lives of all of us and deals with living conditions in every section of the country.
The minister said a moment ago that the budget had been called different names. That is quite the usual thing. We have heard it called a sunshine budget, an election budget, a sunset budget, a rich man's budget, and the other day I heard someone call it a moonshine budget. I think that is a very appropriate term to apply to it because it shed a very dim light of hope for most people so far as reduction of the great burden of taxation is concerned. The budget was well presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and was greatly applauded by the government supporters. It sounded good at that time, but I fear that the enthusiasm which was general then was very short-lived. I am sure that many supporters of the government are now wondering just what they were applauding at that time.
Even corporations, which received the most benefit, are dubious about those benefits because there is no cut in expenditure which would give the tax cuts a dependable foundation. A brief presented by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) a short time ago reads in part as follows:
Economy and efficiency in government is as essential to the economic health of the country as economy and efficiency in business is to the health of business. The executive council therefore feels that a searching examination of government

expenditures in all departments should be made. Even small economies are important, because they tend to develop within government and its administration a cost consciousness, and if there are enough of them they have a cumulative effect which can be substantial.
To them, if this is meant to be a businessman's budget, the basis of the relief it offers -tax cuts without economy-may appear rather unbusinesslike.
Mr. Speaker, I might say that I come from a rural constituency, where 80 per cent of my constituents are farmers. I have listened to the protests of the farmer members in this house and I agree with the protests that have been made, that the farmer has received very little as far as this budget is concerned. Added to that, farm prices across Canada are lower, but what farmers are buying today has increased in price in many parts of the country. Now we have an increase in freight rates which will bear very heavily upon the farming population.
In my own province, New Brunswick, there has been a substantial drop in farm prices. I was interested to notice that, according to the dominion bureau of statistics a short time ago, the most serious drop in farm prices has occurred in the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. The index of prices in New Brunswick has dropped 13 - 2 per cent and in Prince Edward Island 12-7 per cent, while the average in Canada was a drop of iV of 1 per cent.
Allied with farming in the maritime provinces, fishing is one of our great industries. I am not going to dwell upon the plight of fishermen this afternoon, as that was ably dealt with by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) a few days ago, except to say that I am heartily in accord with the arguments presented by him. He asked for a reduction in the sales tax, which would have helped and benefited the farmers and fishermen in my province very greatly.
I wish also to approve of the arguments which have been used in favour of some assistance to the municipalities across Canada. I agree that government companies and federal properties should pay taxes to municipalities, and that it would only be fair as well that the machinery which is used by towns, villages and municipalities should be free from sales tax.
I should like to read briefly, Mr. Speaker, from an article which appeared in the Loyalist, a weekly paper published in the city of Saint John, dated March 7. The headline is "New Brunswick municipalities get warning-tax defaults past danger point". The minister of education in that province pointed out that there has been tremendous default

in different municipalities and that it was practically impossible for municipalities to pay their taxes. He issued this warning:
Municipalities were warned that "some of our municipalities may have to take extreme measures to maintain their solvency."
That very well illustrates what the situation is not only in New Brunswick, Mr. Speaker, but all across Canada, as far as municipalities are concerned.
There was appreciation for some relief in certain cases, cigarettes, stamps, radio tax and so on. Those are small reductions and I have no doubt they are appreciated to the extent to which they give relief, but they have been of very little help indeed to the farmers, fishermen and labourers throughout the country. Even the assistance which was given to the corporations does not benefit certain sections of the country as much as it does others. That is quite obvious.
We in the maritime provinces lack great corporations and industries such as are found in the central provinces and, consequently, in that regard we are not receiving anywhere near the benefits that are being received by the central provinces. I might say that, in spite of the fact that we have few industries compared with other parts of Canada-and hon. members from other parts of the maritimes have mentioned this in this debate-we have some outstanding industries that we are proud of, industries which, over a long period of years and in spite of difficulties, have been able to maintain their existence and prosper to a certain extent. I can refer to Ganong's chocolates, in the town of St. Stephen; the Simms' brush factory in the city of Saint John, now three or four generations with that family; the McAvity foundry in the city of Saint John; the Hartt boot and shoe factory in Fredericton, which I am told turns out some of the finest boots in Canada. I do not want to do any advertising for these people-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They deserve it.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -I just want to point out that we have in the maritimes many outstanding industries. We have Red Rose tea and coffee, Stanfield's underwear-

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-the Atlantic sugar refinery and many others. We are not devoid of industries in the maritime provinces, and while we lack them in quantity we certainly have them in quality.
I listened to the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) when he spoke the other day about children's allowances and old age pensions. He indicated that we received back from the central provinces
The Budget-Mr. Brooks considerable money in this connection. Well, I know the people of my own province and I know the people of the other maritime provinces. We do not wish to subsist on old age pensions and children's allowances or other handouts of that kind. What we want and what we need in our province is more industry.
I might say that we in the maritime provinces feel that we have all the essentials there for the carrying on of industry. We have industrious and intelligent people, and I think we have proven that conclusively to all parts of Canada and to many parts of the United States. There is no finer place to live in Canada than down by the sea. We have splendid recreational facilities of all kinds, and we have a delightful climate. All those things should tend to encourage industries to come to those provinces by the sea. However, we have a lack of industry and we have our unemployment problem. The hon. member for Saint John-Albert will bear me out when I say that in the city of Saint John, which is one of our great winter ports, there are many men unemployed this winter because there is a lack of the shipping that we might expect.
The other day I received an answer to a question regarding the immigration sheds in the city of Saint John, and I want to call this matter to the attention of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris). We have a well equipped immigration shed, perhaps the best equipped in Canada, but there is just a trickle of immigrants coming through the port of Saint John. The minister told me last year that the matter would be looked into and would be corrected.
Mention was made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) of the prospects of improving trade with South America. Not long ago I brought up in this house the question of trade with the West Indies. Trade with the West Indies and and with South America is practically the same thing. A few days ago, Mr. Speaker, I was amazed to learn that a line of boats owned by the Canadian National Railways, a government-owned railway, which had been plying between Halifax, Saint John and the West Indies for the past 25 years, was discontinued. If we are to build up trade with the West Indies and South American countries we must have some means of ocean transportation to those countries. In the same newspaper which announced that the "Lady" boats, as we call them in the maritimes, were to be taken off, I was pleased to read that an English company would commence service. I suppose the company was looking forward to this trade which we hope

The Budget-Mr. Brooks to develop with the South American countries. The article announced that the English company, the Lamport and Holt Line, would begin regular calls at Montreal this year.
This is an item taken from the Montreal Gazette of March 10, and it says that the line, which has a fleet of 15 motor and 3 steam vessels, will offer shippers from Montreal service between Montreal and the South American ports of Bahia, Rio de Janeiro, Santos, Montevideo and Buenos Aires. It goes on to say that these vessels will call at the port of Saint John in the winter months. These boats are being brought to Canada by the Canadian Pacific Steamship lines, and not the Canadian National.
I am very pleased to know that this is the case, Mr. Speaker, because I think there are tremendous possibilities for the development of trade between the maritime provinces and the South American countries. We are in a natural position to trade. Transportation by boat is the cheapest kind of transportation. I believe that we have and could manufacture what the South American people would need in the way of manufactured goods, and they have things in other lines that we need.
There is another matter which I should like to mention, Mr. Speaker, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert the other day and has been brought before this house time and time again by members from the maritime provinces. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black), the hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Stanfield), as well as practically every maritime member in this house, have spoken of the need for more hydroelectric power in the maritimes. I recall that during the war I asked the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) why the maritime provinces had not received more orders for defence production. His reply at that time was that we did not have the electric power with which to produce the goods. The greatest lack today in the economy of the maritime provinces is this hydroelectric power.
It is not necessary for me to tell what benefits power can bring. The great pulp and paper industry in the northern part of our province is due to the hydroelectric power development at Grand Falls. It has provided many people with employment and has built up such towns as Edmundston, Campbellton, Dalhousie and Bathurst, the home of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud). We need more hydroelectric power.
TMt. Brooks.]

The other day the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) mentioned the possibility of New Brunswick developing hydroelectric power on the Saint John river. I do not know how far this plan has gone or just what development there might be. I do know that just before the election in New Brunswick a plan was outlined, I think as election propaganda. What will be done later I do not know.
There is one thing I should like to say, and I am sorry the hon. member for Temiscouata is not here; that is that we in New Brunswick have no intention of hurting in any way the province of Quebec. We would not bully the province of Quebec for anything, and so far as the constituency of Temiscouata is concerned we have no intention of building dams to flood that beautiful constituency. There are no people more kindly disposed towards the people of Quebec than are the people of New Brunswick, because we are next door neighbours. I believe there is more interchange between our peoples than between any other sections of the country.
Now I come to what I have advocated a number of times in this house, and that is the development of power at Passamaquoddy. Whether or not such a plan is feasible is not known at the present time. For many years the people of New Brunswick have dreamed of harnessing these tremendous tides in the bay of Fundy, which rise to a height of 40 feet or more and which come in with their tremendous force twice a day. It has been a dream, as I say, of our people that this tremendous power could be harnessed for the benefit of our people and for the creation of industry. In 1950 there was an investigation by the international joint commission into the scope and costs of the Passamaquoddy tidal power project. I should like to quote a paragraph or two from the report of this commission, at page 4:
It is the opinion of the board that an international Passamaquoddy tidal power development can be physically engineered, constructed, and operated. However, information now available is not adequate to permit determination of its economic feasibility.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert spoke about this the other day. He said he hoped a further investigation would be made as to the economic feasibility of the project. This report goes on to say:
An investigation to determine the economic feasibility for any plan of tidal power development at Passamaquoddy bay should consider: (1) all possible types, arrangements and capacities of tidal power development:	(2) co-ordination with
auxiliary hydroelectric and/or pumped storage projects and with existing power systems: (3) potential known and possible new power markets for the project output;

I shall not read them all.
(5) the effect of a tidal power project on the fisheries of the region;
That is one very important aspect of the project, and one of the objections which New Brunswick has taken to the development of this tidal power plan, that it may adversely affect the fisheries of the province.
Then I quote paragraph 15:
15. The scope of such an investigation is described in detail in part III of this report and its cost is estimated at about $3,900,000.
That is what it would cost Canada and the United States to make an investigation into the economic feasibility of the development of hydroelectric power at Passama-quoddy. Of this $3,900,000, $300,000 would be for the investigation to ascertain the effect of the project on the fisheries of that area. I should like to quote from page 8 of the report what the commission said about the effect on the fisheries. It states:
The herring population is produced beyond the influence of local mixing and no way has been foreseen by which the dam would render the outer Quoddy region or the bay of Fundy less favourable to the existence of herring arriving from elsewhere.
And later on:
There appears little probability of the proposed dams affecting the sardine fishery along the coast of Maine or even seriously at Grand Manan.
Then a little later in the report:
During the years 1930 and 1931 the commercial herring catch for Passamaquoddy and Cobscook bays inside the proposed dam form 2-5 per cent-
Note that, Mr. Speaker; just 2.5 per cent. *-and the areas outside the dams from St. Mary bay, Nova Scotia, to Cape Elizabeth, Maine 97-5 per cent of that for the whole region.
From this report, then, it would look as though the argument which has been used in my province for a good many years against this development-namely that it would affect the fisheries-would not stand up on a thorough investigation. However, this report asks for and recommends an investigation; and I think one should be made.
I should like to say something about the attitude of Canada and the United States to this further investigation of Passamaquoddy power. I have here a letter from Hon. Margaret Smith, United States senator for the state of Maine. She wrote me on February 9 in reply to a letter of inquiry I sent to her. She says in part:
Washington is very interested in the Quoddy proposal. However, there is a general impression that Canada has a relatively negative attitude on the proposal-and that impression is acting somewhat to the prejudice of the proposal. I hope that is not true and that you can help to clear up the matter.
The Budget-Mr. Brooks She also sent me a copy of a joint resolution, presented by herself, which is now before the senate of the United States and is getting the support of practically all the New England senators, all the congressmen from the New England states and, I understand, receiving quite general support in the senate. I might say that ex-President Truman and the late President Roosevelt agreed that this waterpower development, if feasible, should be gone ahead with. In a letter that I received from Senator Smith on March 6 she had this to say.
Let me assure you that we will keep plugging on this side-hoping that you and Mr. Riley and those in Canada who share your views can bring about a change in the official attitude of the Canadian government.
That seems to be the sticking point, Mr. Speaker, as far as the further investigation is concerned, namely that our Canadian government, not the United States government, is opposing it. Senator Smith sent me a copy of a letter dated December 3, 1952, in reply to a letter which she had sent to the Department of State in Washington. The letter reads as follows:
*wiy aear senator Smith:
With reference to your letter of November 19, 1952, concerning Canadian participation in the proposed Passamaquoddy project investigation, Canadian officials told the State department informally on December 2, 1952, that the Canadian government would probably grant permission to the United States government for the surveys in Canadian waters which are anticipated in connection with the Passamaquoddy survey. Permission would have to be sought through formal diplomatic channels.
It was also stated informally that the Canadian government is not interested in sharing the cost of the surveys or any part thereof. Lack of Canadian interest is related to the determination of that government that the power needs of the areas of Canada which would be affected can best be met y smaller installations involving more reasonable amounts #of power and lower costs.
I do not know what authority the federal government has to make that statement, Mr. Speaker. I know, however, that for years we have been asking for power, and I know that for years we have been without it. Despite the fact that the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) the other day said that we had power enough, I know that we have not. We in the maritimes are starving for electric power. With the great developments which we have every reason to expect in connection with our mineral resources, we shall need more and more power. For instance, we do not want these base metals which are being found in large quantities in the province of New Brunswick, to be shipped away in their raw state. We want our own smelters down there. We want our base metals to be refined and smelted in our own refineries and our own, smelters.
2886	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Brooks This can only be done if our province has more electric power.
I am not going to dwell on that subject any longer, but I hope that the government will accede to the wishes of the members from New Brunswick and the other maritime provinces, and will make an investigation of this Quoddy project. It is not going to cost much. They will have the assistance of the United States government; and according to reports the United States is anxious to go ahead with the investigation.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say there is a matter which I shall just touch on for a few moments because it has been dealt with by many others in the house during this debate and at other times. I refer to the war veterans allowance and the ceiling in connection with it. Last year in the veterans affairs committee this matter was brought to the attention of the government. We urged the government to increase the ceiling. We pointed out that it was a great injustice to war veterans that the ceiling was so low. As a matter of fact, before the amendment in 1952 the ceiling was higher than it was after the act had been amended that year. The former ceiling was $125 for single veterans. It allowed income over and above the allowance of $125 for a single man and $250 for a married couple. Now the ceiling is $120 for a single man and $120 for a married couple. It does not allow a war veteran any opportunity at all to earn money on the side.
The government felt they were doing a grand thing when they put in the War Veterans Allowance Act section 4, which permitted war veterans to earn money on a monthly basis and provided that then, after they had worked a number of months, they could return again to the war veterans allowance. The government thought that provision was going to satisfy large numbers of war veterans and more or less take the place of other improvements which we had asked for. On March 3 I asked the question of the Department of Veterans Affairs:
How many veterans receiving war veterans allowance have taken advantage of section 4 War Veterans Allowance Act, as of March 1, 1953?
The answer is that out of 29,998-practically 30,000 men-in receipt of war veterans allowance, only 258 took advantage of section 4; or in other words only 258 were working on a monthly basis. That, in itself, shows that the recipient of the war veterans allowance has reached the age where it is practically impossible for him to do a full day's work.


Today the average age of the veteran is, I believe, over 60 years. I do contend that these men should have received more consideration last year at the hands of the government, and of our war veterans committee. I	hope the government will
again set	up	a war veterans committee so that amendments can be made to the War Veterans Allowance Act, raising the ceiling so these men may be allowed to earn more money while at the same time taking advantage of their allowances.
I have noted a number of cases which to my mind show injustice. First there is the veteran who is not able to do a full day's work, but who could handle a part-time job, such as that of janitor in a small school or church. Perhaps, with his wife, they could take in boarders. But the difficulty is that if they earn over $120 the war veterans allowance is decreased by that amount.
Then there is the thrifty and prudent man who has earned for himself a small retirement pension of $25 or $30 a month from some organization for which he worked. I am not in this instance referring to the veterans' pension. But again, his war veterans allowance is reduced. If he is married he is not allowed to receive more than $1,200 a year or, if single, $720.
Then there is the case of the disability pensioner. If he is entitled to the war veterans allowance and receives more than a 50 per cent pension, he gets very little assistance. The single veteran with a 50 per cent pension receives no assistance whatever. The other day I received a letter from a veteran in my constituency, whose wife was also a veteran, having served as a nursing sister during the war. She had incurred some disability and received a 20 per cent pension. When this man was put on the war veterans allowance his wife's 20 per cent pension was reduced because it was contended that the husband and wife were receiving more than the ceiling permitted.
These are all matters which should be brought to the attention of a committee on veterans affairs. I recommend, as I have on many occasions in the house, that a committee on veterans affairs should be set up on a permanent basis to deal with matters of this kind.

maintopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the presentation of the budget Liberal members opposite were loud in their applause. I could not help thinking that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in all probability must have given them a pep talk, reminding them that last year when the budget was brought down there was press comment to the effect that it had been

received in stony silence. Probably he urged them to express appreciation for whatever small concessions might be granted in the budget.
However it seems to me that having had time for sober reflection, Liberal members must admit that there was very little cause for the rejoicing and the hullabaloo of that time. I think it must be clear to them now that some important ingredient was missing from the Abbott brew which, while apparently it had an intoxicating effect upon Liberal members at the time it was served, since that time has not only gone flat but has become decidedly sour.
A great deal has been said during the course of the debate about the taxation proposals. I shall touch upon them only briefly. By many the budget has been called a rich man's budget, and I think that is a fair description of it. Certainly there is very little relief in it for people in the lower income brackets.
In closing his speech this afternoon the minister stated that the budget was based upon the assumption that Canada will remain prosperous throughout 1953. That being so, I think there would have been every reason to reduce taxation upon that class of people who are not able to enjoy that prosperity today. In other words there would have been every justification for making a reduction in the sales tax and the income tax affecting people in the lower income brackets. After all, that would have helped to bolster effective demand.
It will be recalled that in his budget speech the minister pointed out that the demand fell off in the fall of 1951 and the early part of 1952; but that later on, when restrictions on credit buying were removed, demand picked up. Throughout the latter part of 1952 there was a heavy increase in instalment buying, charge accounts and personal loans from chartered banks.
I do not think it is a very healthy situation when certain groups of people have to go into debt in order to buy their daily requirements, especially when the debt increases at a time when there is such a high level of prosperity. Had the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) used the $250 million he had to play around with for the purpose of reducing the sales tax and increasing income tax exemptions, it would have helped to improve the situation.
I should like for a few moments to deal with agriculture. In his budget speech the minister referred to the high level of production, wages and income, and stated he was gratified that this situation had continued at a time when the wholesale price 68108-184
The Budget-Mr. Quelch index had fallen by 7 per cent and the retail price index by 2 per cent. Well, the minister may have been gratified, but he cannot expect agriculture to share his gratification when we consider the fact that practically the whole of the drop in the wholesale price index can be traced to the fact that the wholesale price index on agricultural products had fallen by 17 per cent.
Attention is drawn to this fact by the governor of the Bank of Canada in his annual report for the year 1952 wherein, at page 2, he says:
Livestock production also increased; there was an abundant supply of meat on the domestic market and prices fell considerably, accounting for about the whole of the decline during 1952 in the consumer price index. Export markets for livestock and meat, however, were limited following the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease early in 1952.
While the Minister of Finance may have been gratified to see the fall in the wholesale price index, he could not expect the livestock growers in this country to be gratified, when the fall in the prices they received was solely responsible for the reduction in the wholesale price level, and especially at a time when their costs of operation were rising.
When the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was speaking he indicated that he did not like comparisons being made between 1952 and 1951. He pointed out that in 1951 we had a record in both production and gross income for agriculture. My point is that when the Minister of Agriculture referred to the record production and prices for agricultural products he did not point out that while there had been a large gross income for farmers, the cost of production had increased considerably during that period.
I want to point out that 1951 was not by any means the best year for agriculture, as indicated by the Minister of Agriculture. The best period which agriculture has had in Canada was between 1916 and 1920. During that period the farmers of Canada, representing 30 per cent of the population, received 30 per cent of the national income. In other words, from 1916 to 1920 agriculture received a parity of income. In 1951 the farmers, representing around 20 per cent of the population, received only about 10 per cent of the national income.
If we take the years 1916 to 1920 as a base period, according to figures obtained from the bureau of statistics we find that in 1949 the index for the price of wheat was 87, while the index for the prices of farm machinery was 209. By 1950 the index for the prices of farm machinery had increased to 218 while the price of wheat had fallen

The Budget-Mr. Quelch due to the exchange rate on the dollar. The Minister of Agriculture pointed out that there was no change in the price of farm machinery in 1951 and therefore the index can be taken to remain at 218, but as hon. members know the price of wheat fell still further on account of the Canadian dollar going up in relation to the United States dollar so that the index for the price of wheat in 1951 would be below 87.
The Minister of Agriculture made quite a point of the fact that farm machinery represents only from 8 to 9 per cent of the costs incurred by agriculture as a whole. That may be true of agriculture as a whole, but if you take the highly mechanized state of western agriculture you find that machine costs are greatly in excess of 8 or 9 per cent of the cost of raising wheat. If you consider other commodities which enter into the cost of farming you find a situation similar to that with regard to machinery. For instance, wages have gone up considerably since the period 1916-20. Freight rates have gone up over 100 per cent in the past five years. Fuel for tractors has gone up, and in addition taxes have increased considerably since that period.
The Minister of Agriculture tried to substantiate his claim that the period during the post-war years had been exceptionally good, and he made a comparison between that period and six years before the war. I think it is important to remember that the six years immediately prior to the war were the last six years of a ten-year depression. During that period western Canada suffered a serious drought. It was a period during which many farmers were practically in a state of bankruptcy. During that period, in order to maintain their actual living costs, farmers allowed their capital and machinery to depreciate considerably. A farmer cannot operate efficiently when he allows his capital to depreciate. At the same time purchasing power in Canada was at a low level, thus reducing the domestic market for agricultural products.
When the minister compares the six postwar years with the six years of the depression he is not making a very sound comparison. If the Minister of Agriculture had really been interested in making a sound comparison he should have compared during the past five years the relationship between the prices received for agricultural products and the costs of production. If he had done that he would have found a very different picture from the one he gave.
During his speech the Minister of Agriculture referred many times to the federation


of agriculture and pointed out that in his opinion their criticisms, generally speaking, were fair. I should like to quote from an article referring to the annual convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture held this year at Victoria, British Columbia. The Western Farm Leader of February 6 contains the following:
"For those who have the erroneous impression that farmers have been enjoying unprecedented prosperity," said Mr. Hannam, "it would be well to restate the fact that the farmer's income depends not upon prices alone, but farm prices in relation to farm costs. In recent years, farm costs have risen more than farm prices.
"Based on price relationship, the farmer's purchasing power, if represented by the index of 100 in 1948, has been less every year since. For 1952 it stands at 82. Since it is generally agreed that farm prices may be down somewhat and farm costs are expected to hold or go a little higher, this farm purchasing power relationship may well drop to 80 or less during 1953, down by 20 per cent or more since 1948."
That is an important point that must always be taken into consideration when you are assessing the position of agriculture. You must at all times keep in mind the relationship between farm prices and farm costs. When you have a period in which farm prices are falling while farm costs are rising, you do not have a very healthy situation.
We depend a great deal upon the United States for markets for our products. Therefore it is important to farmers in this country to know what happens in the United States. I have here the Alberta Wheat Pool Budget of February 27, 1953 which quotes an article entitled "Farmers Being Squeezed" which appeared in the U. S. News and World Report, a magazine which is quoted quite often in the house by ministers. This article reads in part as follows:
Farmers, even with government help, are in a squeeze right now.
A farmer, on the average, in 1953, will get a smaller proportion of the national income than in any years since the depression bottom in 1932. He will have many more dollars than in 1932, but relative to other parts of the population, his share of the total will be back at a low level.
Put it this way: One person out of six in the country is a farmer. In 1946, when times were best for farmers, $1 out of $9 in national income went to the farmer. In 1953, $1 in $15 will go to the farmer.
Then another matter of interest to the Canadian farmer is the future agricultural policy of the new United States government. I think it will be of great interest to note a statement made by President Eisenhower, and I quote from the overseas report on agricultural developments, economics division, marketing service, Department of Agriculture, which contains the following on page 4:
Some changes, perhaps of a substantial and1 fundamental nature, may be made in agricultural policies by the new Republican administration. In

his state of the union message to Congress on February 2, President Eisenhower referred to the slow, irregular decline in farm prices which has been going on for two years, and promised that prices of basic commodities will be supported at 90 per cent of parity until the end of 1954 . . . We should begin now to consider what farm legislation we should develop for 1955 and beyond. Our aims should be economic stability and full parity of income for American farmers.
I hope the Liberal government will give due consideration to that statement because that is something we have never been able to get the government in this country to recognize, the right of the Canadian farmer to a parity of income. President Eisenhower states that support prices will be continued until 1954, and then the administration will try to devise a policy which will give the American farmers not merely 90 per cent of parity but 100 per cent.
Every time the question of parity is brought up with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) he says he does not like the use of that term because it can mean so many different things. But you cannot dispute what parity of income means. Parity of price may mean several things, but parity of income means one thing and one thing only; that the farmer will receive his fair share of the national income in proportion to the population.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when we take into consideration the situation in the United States and the fact that we in Canada are having difficulty in selling to the United Kingdom because of their lack of dollars and, as the Minister of Agriculture pointed out, because of the price level in that country, then I say there is every reason for concern on the part of our farmers with respect to the present situation.
What is the advice given by the Minister of Agriculture at the present time to the farmers of this country in order to deal with that situation? He emphasizes the importance of the home market, and I am sure we all agree how important the home market is and that everything possible should be done to maintain the purchasing power of the people in the home market at a high level. Then he suggests that farmers should actually reduce their production of certain commodities so as to be less dependent upon the world market.
Last year, when he addressed the annual convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at Montreal, he advised farmers not to increase their production of certain farm commodities, mainly livestock and dairy products; but when he addressed the conven-, tion this year he went even further. He did not merely advise farmers not to increase 68108-184J
The Budget-Mr. Quelch their production; he advised farmers to actually reduce their production in order to get a better price. Again I will quote from the Western Farm Leader of February 6 which contains the following:
Mr. Gardiner stated that the government can get our farm products into the United Kingdom market tomorrow, if we are willing to meet the competition of beef from Argentina at 16 cents a pound and bacon from Denmark at 31-5 cents. Rather than coax farmers to produce things they cannot sell at prices that pay, the proper thing, the minister said, is to produce less for more money.
Before passing on, I would point out that while the figures he gave as to the prices paid by Great Britain for Argentine products may have been correct at the time he spoke, they are not correct today because there is a report in the same issue of the same paper of a new agreement signed between Argentina and the British government, which report reads as follows:
Meat Prices under New Argentine Agreement
Under their new trade agreement with the Argentine, Britain will pay 20*1 cents (U.S.) per pound for top quality frozen beef sides, 22-6 cents for chilled beef, 18-5 for lamb, and 32-8 for pork cuts. Argentina is to take manufactured goods from Britain in exchange.
In other words this is a barter deal. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, there is no question that we in this country could greatly expand our exports of farm products to Great Britain if we were willing to do the same as Argentina and accept British goods in exchange for Canadian products or, if we are not prepared to do that, at least to accept sterling in payment which could be utilized for the purpose of buying goods produced anywhere within the sterling area.
I want to make it plain that I am not for one minute criticizing the Minister of Agriculture for giving that advice, because no doubt he considers it the only way in which farmers can protect themselves under existing government policy. But on the other hand I would bitterly criticize a government policy which makes it necessary to reduce the production of any commodity at a time when there are millions of people in the world on the verge of starvation. I would criticize that policy on two main grounds; first as an anti-social policy, and second because I believe it will greatly weaken the agricultural program in western Canada.
I wonder if I could call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.	.
On motion of Mr. Quelch the debate was adjourned.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad the minister made a short statement, though I thought he would make a much longer one. I am pleased to see that there is a surplus for the Canadian National Railways, but I imagine that surplus is due to the new capitalization.

speechtext:
The recapitalization does put the Canadian National Railways on a little better footing with the Canadian Pacific Railway. That was the intention. It makes things much better for the Canadian National Railways because I think it will give the employees a little better star to shoot at than they had before, when they really had an anchor around their necks all the time.
I am in hopes that now the Canadian National Railways have a surplus they will go out and try to improve the lines more than they have in the past, especially the passenger lines. I do not think that in the past they have gone after business the way they should have. In the past ten or fifteen years the people of Canada have gradually moved over to buses. Although the war did hamper the railways, I feel that the trend is partly accounted for by the fact that the railways have not built up their passenger service the way they should.
In a return that was tabled here I was very pleased to see that Canadian National Railways have bought some 141 new passenger cars. I believe they are buying some in foreign countries, and are spending $32i million on new passenger cars which are being built here in Canada. It is too bad they are not all being built here in Canada, but I imagine that the company is anxious to get these new passenger cars in service as quickly as possible.
The line from Ottawa to Toronto goes through my home city of Peterborough. On that line we have some mighty poor passenger cars.

I hope they never ship them to the maritimes, because if your railway lines are not much better than ours you will not have many passengers travelling on them. Coming in on Monday I noticed that on one line they are using diesel engines, mostly for the freight service. I think the Canadian Pacific Railway is doing the same thing. I hope, and I know, that these diesel engines will make a big difference. The electric components of diesel electric engines are made in my own home town, and many improvements

are being made on those engines all the time.
I expect that in a very short time-some say 15 years and some say 30 years-there will not be any steam locomotives on the railways at all. I hope they will ship the steam locomotives out of the country or junk them and that they won't send them to the maritimes.

They want them for their potatoes, yes. A diesel, however, pays for itself in the saving of fuel within three and a half to five years. That fact ought to help the overhead of different railway companies, and especially the Canadian National Railways, making it possible for the latter to continue to have a surplus.
Mr. Speaker, this committee will also deal with the accounts of Trans-Canada Air Lines. I noticed ini an article in the Gazette of March 11 that a Mr. Richard Lewis, of the trade paper Canadian Broadcaster and Television, stated that the Trans-Canada Air Lines fares on the 348-mile run from New York to Montreal, where they are in competition with a private United States air line, are $3.75 less than on the run from Montreal to Toronto. That run is 11 miles shorter than the New York to Montreal run. On the Toronto to Montreal run, however, Trans-Canada are not in competition with any other company. They have a monopoly and, therefore, they are charging the Canadian people $3.75 more than on the other run. This is not fair to Canadians, because Canadians own Trans-Canada Air Lines. I hope that in the committee I may be able to convince the officials of Trans-Canada Air Lines that this fare should be reduced to make it the same or less than the Montreal to New York fare.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I will have a lot more to say in the committee, but I do not want to detain the house any longer.

speechtext:
About a year ago, on another occasion in this house, I gave some support to the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall), who introduced an item of legislation with which I found myself partially in agreement. Now I find myself in agreement with him again, and I hope this means he is right, because that has an intimate bearing on my position as well. When I heard the hon. member mention the question of sleeping car reservations about a week or two ago, I wondered whether or not the situation was as bad as it was then described. Because I was interested in the matter I made some investigation myself, and found that the hon. member had rather accurately pictured the situation.
I want to tell the minister that the Canadian National-I suppose the Canadian Pacific isi in exactly the same position-is losing scads of money on these sleeping car reservations. I think it is a scandal that the situation has continued as long as it has. I have spoken with sleeping car conductors and others who are interested in this subject, but of course they are governed entirely by the policy of the railway. When the committee meets I think that is one of the things that ought to be dealt with. I am not a member of the committee, and that is the reason I raise the subject here; it is the only opportunity I shall have.
Apparently what happens is this. People reserve these lower berths, bedrooms and the like, and then they have reservations on the plane as well. If the plane happens to make the trip, that is the last the railway hears of the reservation. It is still there on the books, however. I suppose if these people are good customers the railways do not like to be too tough. The result is that the railway carries that reservation, although the man is perhaps at his destination before the train leaves the station. This berth is kept for him, and that accommodation is wasted so far as revenue to the railway is concerned. I would not be at all surprised if the minister found that the railways were losing somewhere between 10 and 15 per cent of their sleeping car revenues through this rather stupid policy, if I may call it that, in connection with reservations. I am amazed that the railways have allowed the situation to continue as long as it has.
So far as the commuters around Montreal and Toronto are concerned, the railways put up a great story about losing money on commuter traffic. I want to say that they need
2892	HOUSE OF
Committee on Railways and Shipping not be so self-righteous about saving money so far as the poor commuters are concerned when they throw money out the window on these sleeping car accommodations. I feel rather keenly about that, because frankly I always had the idea that somehow or other you could only reserve sleeping car accommodation until a certain hour. For instance, if you were leaving at night on the 11 o'clock train, I understood you had to get your sleeping car ticket before 3 o'clock in the afternoon. I believe that is the policy the railway followed with me. I am now wondering if I am being singled out for special attention. Apparently one does not have to pick up the tickets by 3 o'clock, but can let the matter go right up until the time the train leaves. The railway officials do not bother you.
People call up and ask for accommodation on a certain train on a certain night, and they are told that the railway cannot give them accommodation that night because all the sleeping car space is taken. Of course it is reserved, but it is not filled when the train leaves.
I believe the member for Vancouver-Burrard has a very important point. I should like to know, and I think the committee would be able to find out, just how much is being lost through this foolish system of reservations. This will be notice to the railway officials when they come before the committee that they ought to tell the committee, and through that committee the House of Commons, just what the situation is. If this reservation business is conducted largely as a matter of accommodation for customers, then it should not be followed to the stage where the railways are carrying empty berths for long distances across Canada. In many instances these people seem to be so thoughtless that they are not even courteous enough to notify the railways that the berths are not going to be needed. I think that is something the railways ought to consider.
I have no doubt that if the railways have a surplus of $186,000 now, they would have about twice that much if they ever collected the fares for this empty space that is carried on so many trains. What makes me particularly concerned is that, while we are fighting for some justice for the commuters, the railways talk about the losses they have and then allow the loss of revenue from this waste space to continue. I think that is not quite fair. If we ever go before the board of transport commissioners again in connection with commutation rates, the railways need not expect us to swallow all that talk

COMMONS	[
about cutting expenses to the bone and getting every five-cent piece of revenue they can, because it looks to me as though this is revenue they are losing which they do not need to lose, and which, if it were accumulated over the years, it seems to me would amount to a rather immense sum of money. If this is any indication or any pattern of how the railways run their business in some other ways, may I say that I do not think much of it. I wanted to make that just as clear as I could tonight because when the committee meets, I hope its members will take up that matter.

speechtext:
I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that I welcome the setting up of this committee for several reasons. I have been making representations to the railroads, particularly to Mr. Gordon, the president of the Canadian National Railways, in regard to areas of free express delivery in our city of Saskatoon. Like other cities, Saskatoon has been growing rapidly and there are certain districts which are now, I think, entitled to delivery from the railroads free of charge. I am glad to say that matter has been straightened out and that Mr. Gordon has informed me by letter and I have also been so informed by the transit board, if that is the correct term, that these free deliveries will now take place in the south corner of the city. That is one matter which we shall not have to take up in the committee.
I have been greatly interested in this discussion in regard to the demotion of Mr. Pitt. That issue has been a live one in my city for the last few months. I have a large file on it. I welcome the setting up of the committee so that we may have there the proper witnesses who may be questioned in regard to that particular matter.
The minister has taken the position, as have others, that this is a matter of internal management. While one must admit that to a certain extent that is true, at the same time we must remember that, after all, the C.N.R. is a public body. I am not interested in Mr. Pitt's case personally; I have never met the gentleman. But I am interested in seeing that any servant of the government of this country or of any corporation of the government in this country should receive justice and that, when he is dismissed or demoted, he should have good reasons given therefor.
I think I am safe in saying to the minister and of the minister that he has committed himself rather strongly in this particular matter, not only in reply to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) this afternoon but to me and, I fancy, to others who have written to him personally with regard

to the demotion of Mr. Pitt. The minister's position being what it is, there is ah insinuation there. It may not prove to be an insinuation; it may be unfounded in fact. But as far as I am concerned-and I have a large file on the matter-I have not been able to find anything against Mr. Pitt in this matter. The minister, if I may quote from his letter, shows that caution which is exhibited at all times by my honourable and learned friends when he says:
It may well be that the reasons for the transfer of Mr. Pitt, if made public, would react unfavourably to his cause.
Of course I should have to admit that; and Mr. Pitt is in the unfortunate position that he is an employee of the railroad and to that extent his mouth is closed. But those who are intimately in contact with Mr. Pitt tell me that Mr. Pitt has nothing to fear from any investigation. I would express the hope that before that committee we may have those witnesses who can be questioned on this matter in order that we may get the thing cleared up once and for all.
May I say that I do not put any particular stock in the assertion that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), as Prime Minister, had anything to do with this particular matter.
I have more respect for the Prime Minister than to think he would be mixed up in any such affair. But I think that there are lesser men who like to show a large authority. I hope that the facts may be elicited before this committee, and I hope the correct witnesses may be called with regard to the matter. For instance, I would suggest Mr. Pickersgill be called. His official position,
I understand, is that of secretary to the cabinet; and I would also suggest that Mr. Sommerville be called. I understand that he is general manager of C.N.R. hotels throughout Canada.
I am aware that there is a long story behind this thing, which goes away back to the wartime when Mr. Pitt went out on the service of his country, and to the time when he came back and found another man in the position which he would have expected to fill.
I expect there is rivalry there. I expect there is a long story which I cannot go into here. As I say, I have much information on the subject. But I want to say this. In my own city of Saskatoon Mr. Pitt was considered to be a public servant above reproach, a man who gave excellent public service.
I made some inquiries with regard to the employees at the Bessborough hotel where Mr. Pitt was manager. Those people are unanimously in support of Mr. Pitt's cause in this particular issue. I can find nothing against him. On the other hand I found a good deal of criticism with regard to the
12, 1953	2893
Committee on Railways and Shipping man who has been in charge, if I may put it that way, of Mr. Pitt's destinies over the last few years. So far as I am concerned, I am not satisfied with things as they are. Whatever the truth is, let us get at it. Let us have the thing out. Let us have these witnesses before the committee.
I know the government has had lots of notice about this thing. The hon. member for Lake Centre raised the matter in the house. I think I myself raised it perhaps first of all. The government have had lots of time to prepare their case. All right, let them prepare their case, and let them be prepared to submit it to a public tribunal, this committee, when it is set up.
I am not interested in Mr. Pitt as a senior man in the service. I am interested that the humblest man in the public service of this country, whoever he may be, should receive justice from the people for whom he works. That is what I am interested in. I hope this committee will reveal the truth, whatever it may be, let the chips fall where they may.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT-OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one member of this committee I should like to bring a few matters to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). One of them is this. For the benefit of the members of this committee, the reports should be in their hands at as early a date as possible. Last year I think the reports were not in the hands of the members until a couple of days before the committee sat. There is no reason why we should not have those reports at least fifteen days before the sitting of the committee.
The next matter is this, and I do not know whether the Minister of Transport would care to say anything about it or not. What is the reason for these large orders for cars going outside of Canada? I refer to the new cars that are going to be made. After waiting for years, I do not think the company needs to be in such a great hurry to get this equipment. I believe that procurement could be distributed over a certain period of time in order to provide employment in our own country. Surely Canadian companies can make as good cars for the railways as can any other companies in America.
Another matter I should like to draw to the attention of the minister is that the returns given with regard to the operations of each division are very general indeed. We have never been able to get returns on eastern or western divisions, or even our own division in Prince Edward Island. The convenience of having those returns would be worth something to our shippers, and to the committee in general. They would give
2894	HOUSE OF
Committee on Railways and Shipping definite proof whether the operation of diesel engines is a good thing financially.
Last season the only information we had was as the result of a direct question I asked the president, when he gave us to understand that $300,000 was saved by dieselizing the Prince Edward Island railway. If we had a statement for the whole railway system showing the present operating expenses as compared with what they used to be, perhaps it would be one of their best arguments for the dieselization of the whole Canadian National Railways system.
No doubt the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) is aware of the fact that the hotel employees are now ready to go on a grand strike all across Canada. Perhaps this is only a scare put out ini order to bring the pay of hotel employees up to a better standard, and also to have shorter hours. Perhaps the minister would be prepared to urge upon the hotel employees' association that, if at all possible, a strike should be avoided. The railways have not yet been notified of any final date set for the calling of the strike.
Then I suggest that we are entitled to more information in connection with the operation of the ferry service between Borden and Tormentine. This service is operated by the Canadian National Railways. The only bookkeeping of which we are aware is that they pay themselves their own subsidy. I suggest we should be shown a statement of the earnings of that ferry service. It must be a paying proposition, because I understand the Canadian National Railways now have their eyes glued on a private enterprise ferry operating between Wood island and Caribou. They are anxious to get control of this ferry service, and thus have a monopoly of that means of transportation. I hope the minister will never permit or assist the Canadian National Railways to get control of all our ferry service, especially this independent line that is giving one of the best services that has ever been given ini that capacity.
In closing I would express the hope that I have not asked any questions I should not have asked at this time. If I have, then it is within the minister's power to refrain from answering.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the minister replies there is one point I would ask him to clear up in connection with the powers and privileges of the committee. The impression the house and country may have gathered from the statement made yesterday by the minister may have been that the committee to be set up would be entitled to the production of certain letters. I think we should know whether it is 

the minister's position that those letters not only may be but will be produced in the committee, if we ask for them, or whether in the committee we will be entitled only to a statement from the president of the Canadian National Railways.
Obviously it is going to have a very important bearing upon the position of hon. members in the committee-the decision as to whether or not they will ask for that information-if we are to be provided only with a statement from the president of the Canadian National Railways, following which we will have no opportunity to demand the production of the documents, the letters, on the basis of which he makes this decision. Because if that is so, then obviously there is no reason why we should ask for the information.
We have found frequently in committee that we ask for information and are presented with statements on which we have no opportunity for effective cross-examination. We find we have no opportunity to require the production of documents upon which that statement is based. Yesterday, as I heard him, the minister gave the impression, at first at any rate, that the committee would be entitled to a full disclosure of all the facts surrounding the case of the former manager of the Fort Garry hotel.
I suggest we should have a statement from the minister at this point, before the debate closes, stating whether, if we ask for it, we are going to be provided with the correspondence, on the basis the minister stated in the house yesterday. Because if we are not going to have the letters, then I think it should be made perfectly clear that no member is to be criticized because he does not go in there and ask the president of the C.N.R. to make a statement which we will have no opportunity to refute.
