speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to hon. members for the short discussion which has just taken place on the establishment of the committee, a discussion which I believe will serve a useful purpose.
Many questions have been put to me, and I am sure the house will not expect that I should deal with all of them; because the purpose of the committee is to consider many of the questions which have been asked here this evening. To answer some of them would take considerable time, and I think I should leave to the officers of the railways, whose duty and business it is to deal with these matters, the responsibility of replying

to most of the queries which have been directed to me.
However, there are some questions to which I feel I should refer. One of these was mentioned by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gi'llis). He referred to a statement made by the minister of labour of his province who said that he hoped a delay would take place in the dieselization program of the Canadian National Railways.
All I can say with regard to that is that the minister of labour came to Ottawa with a delegation from the maritime provinces to see the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) and myself. They made many representations, among which was this particular one asking for a delay in the dieselization program. I had to say to that delegation that this was a matter for the management of the Canadian National Railways, and that I would bring it to the attention of the officials of the railroad. That I have done.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) is familiar with the position taken by the Canadian National Railways in previous committees, and the program that was announced then. I do not think I should attempt to anticipate what the president of the Canadian National Railways will say, and I would prefer to leave this matter for him when he comes before the committee.
Some questions were asked about equipment purchased in the United States. As the house knows, the Canadian National Railways follows the practice of asking for tenders for equipment. The date of delivery in the tender has a great deal to do with the granting of the order. In the instance mentioned by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) and the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) I believe a substantial portion of the orders went to Canadian firms because they were the lowest tenderers and the date of delivery was satisfactory. Substantial orders also went to United States firms because they were the lowest in their submissions and also because of the time factor. There is another point to be considered, in that some of this equipment will be used on the United States lines of the Canadian National Railways.
The question was asked about fares charged by T.C.A. on movements to the United States and between Toronto and Montreal. As the house knows, I am not the minister responsible for the operations of Trans-Canada Air Lines, but I can say that the tariff of fares charged by the various air
12, 1953	2895
Committee on Railways and Shipping lines are subject to approval by the air transport board. Tariffs must be filed with that board after notice has been given to competitors and to the public. Fares are determined, sometimes after a public hearing and sometimes without a hearing. I can say to my hon. friend that presumably the fares in this case would be determined on the basis of differential because of competition. I imagine that my hon. friend will want to raise this question when the president of T.C.A. is before the committee.

speechtext: Surely the government determines whether there will be competition.

Then again there is another point. Is the traffic on the transcontinental route heavy enough to warrant another operator, such as the C.P.A., coming in? That is a matter to which the government and the air transport board must give consideration. Up until now it has been felt that the T.C.A. should continue to operate on the transcontinental route while the other competitors should operate on the north-south routes.
Other questions were asked by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), and I understand the other evening by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall). My hon. friends will excuse me if I do not deal with these questions, but they cover matters

Committee on Railways and Shipping with which I am not too familiar. I think they should be left for determination by the committee.

The hon. member for Saskatoon said that he had taken a keen interest in the case of the former manager of the Fort Garry hotel. I am glad he has done so, and I hope every facility will be afforded him to obtain the information which he requires. However, he seems to have put this matter on an entirely different footing. He says that Mr. Pitt has nothing to fear from an investigation. I simply repeat in effect what I have said earlier, that the Canadian National Railways has nothing to fear from any investigation. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that the Canada Shipping Act was last amended in 1950. At that time extensive changes were made in the act which were required in order to implement the international convention for the safety of life at sea which was signed in London on July 10,
Canada Shipping Act
1948. That convention came into force on November 19, 1952 with respect to the countries, including Canada, which have ratified it, and the relevant amendments made to the act in 1950 were proclaimed effective December 31, 1952.
The 1929 safety convention will remain effective for one year between Canada and the parties to that convention which have not accepted the 1948 convention. Provision is made in the bill to cover this transitional period. After November 19, 1953, ships of countries which by that time have not accepted the 1948 convention will no longer have the protection in Canadian ports of an international certificate, and consequently will be subject to the requirements of the Canada Shipping Act in respect of safety equipment.
The amendments proposed in the bill which is now before the house are not extensive. The first amendment is technical, relating to certificates issued to engineers on steamships. As defined in the act, the term "steamship" includes ships propelled both by steam and by internal combustion engines. There is a great disparity between the actual power developed by a steam engine and an internal combustion engine. Under section 114 of the act certificates to engineers are based on nominal horsepower, which is the term used in describing the size of the engine but does not correspond to the actual horsepower developed.
It is proposed to amend this section to require engineers on ships propelled by internal combustion engines to have a higher grade of certificate than engineers on ships driven by steam engines of the same nominal horsepower. This will bring a measure of uniformity in the certificates issued to engineers employed on the two classes of ships. Provision is made so that the rights and powers of certificates now issued will not be affected.
The second amendment relates to radiotelegraph and radiotelephone installations. I have indicated on previous occasions that amendments would be introduced relating to radio installations on ships plying coastal waters, particularly on the west coast. Under subsection 2 of section 406 of the act, passenger ships carrying more than 50 passengers and plying on certain coastal voyages such as those on the west coast are required to be equipped with a radiotelegraph installation complying with the provisions of the international safety convention, and to carry the prescribed number of operators. Subsection 2 of section 406 also applies to cargo ships of five thousand gross tons and upwards going

Canada Shipping Act
on voyages of more than two hundred miles from one place to another, unless exempted by the governor in council.
It is proposed to amend this section to require all passenger steamships over sixty-five feet in length going on any voyage outside of a port to be fitted with a radiotelegraph installation complying with the provisions of the safety convention. The amendment provides that radio operators shall not engage in any other duties which in any way interfere with the keeping of watches. Provision is also made for exempting certain vessels where it is expedient to do so, having regard to the nature of the voyage in which the ship is engaged and the radiotelephone installation on the ship, or other circumstances of the case. In the case of ferry ships, or other vessels going on short voyages in protected waters, there would not appear to be the same necessity to carry radiotelegraphy as in the case of ships going on longer voyages in open waters, particularly if these vessels carry radiotelephone.
The proposed amendment also covers cargo steamships of five hundred gross tons and upwards and steamships under five hundred tons engaged in towing another vessel of five hundred tons or over, or towing any. other floating object, such as a raft of logs, having a dimension in any direction of one hundred and fifty feet or more where the vessel towed does not carry radiotelegraph equipment. Provision is made for exemption as it is considered that where these ships are equipped with radiotelephone and are plying on short voyages or in protected waters the provision of a radiotelegraph installation may not be necessary.
At the last session of parliament approval was given to the agreement made between Canada and the United States for the promotion of safety on the great lakes by means of radio. The instruments of ratification have been exchanged between the two governments, and the agreement will come into force in 1954. It is necessary to amend the Canada Shipping Act in order to implement this agreement, and provision is made in the bill for regulations to be made by the governor in council requiring ships navigating on the great lakes and St. Lawrence river above the Lachine canal and the Victoria bridge at Montreal to be equipped with radiotelephone. Broadly speaking, the great lakes agreement covers passenger ships over sixty-five feet in length, cargo ships of five hundred gross tons and upwards, and ships under five hundred gross tons engaged in towing vessels of five hundred gross tons or over where the latter vessel does not carry radiotelephone. 
The third amendment concerns the inspection of tow barges. Under the law as it now stands tow barges that carry passengers are subject to steamship inspection and to the requirements of the act in so far as they are applicable to that type of vessel. Tow barges that carry a crew but not passengers are not subject to inspection. It is considered that tow barges carrying crew but not passengers should be subject to the regulations respecting lifesaving equipment, fire extinguishing equipment, precautions against fire and the provisions of the act relating to inspection of boilers in tow barges. The amendment to section 475 of the act is designed to carry out this purpose.
There are two other minor amendments, one providing for the appointment under the Canada Shipping Act of port wardens and deputy port wardens, and the other relating to the coming into force in Newfoundland of certain excepted provisions of the act.
On the whole, Mr. Speaker, -the amendments proposed in this bill are the result of a study made in the committee, which is a continuing committee in the Department of Transport and which, from time to time, deals with matters affecting the Canada Shipping Act. At times it hears representatives from other bodies too.
When the bill has received second reading I will propose, and I am sure there will be no objection, that it be referred for further study to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speechtext:
The Canada Shipping Act is of the utmost importance to people in all those parts of the country which are interested in shipping. They, of course, include not only Canadians on the east and west coasts but also those living along the St. Lawrence river and on the great lakes. A very large proportion of the Canadian people are directly involved in shipping matters.
This act is very long. It is a whole volume in itself; it is very involved, and the amendments which are proposed require careful study. For that reason I believe the minister is very wise in referring the bill to the committee.

The amendments seem to be beneficial, although there is some uncertainty in my mind as to just how far they go. We have had a great deal of worry on the west coast with regard to the question of passenger ships carrying Marconi operators, referred to in the bill as "radiotelegraph operators". There has been a tendency on the part of some of the shipping companies to make the radiotelegraph operator do other work such as acting as freight checker, part-time purser or engaging in other operations. That meant that he was not devoting his whole time to his instruments and it was a very dangerous trend. The difficulty has arisen partially because of the development of the radiotelephone. Quite a few shipping people thought the radiotelephone might do away with radiotelegraph. I am convinced that such is not a proper step, but I realize that there is some difficulty in working out the respective spheres of these two types of communication.
As I read the bill, discretion has been left pretty largely to the department to decide which ships are to have a radiotelegraph operator and which will be allowed to get by with the radiotelephone. I doubt whether the bill, as it is introduced, defines the spheres in a sufficiently clear manner to be satisfactory for many years. Perhaps it is a matter of trial and error and, as time goes on, we will be able to make the proper division.
However, there is one omission in the bill which I hope the minister will explain when he closes this debate. There is no mention whatever of radar. On our coast the use of radar is becoming quite widespread. It is not entirely satisfactory, and there have been some pretty nasty accidents where the radar was not in operation. I know that steps have been taken on a voluntary basis to train ships' officers in the use of radar; but there is no compulsion about it, and no standards have been set which must be reached in that training. So far as I know there are no regulations under the Canada Shipping Act dealing with the use of radar. It may be that this wonderful invention has not been developed to the stage where regulations can be enacted in respect of it. I would ask the minister to explain just what the present position is with regard to the use of radar on ships.
On the west coast there has been tremendous development. I need only remind members of the great aluminum plant which is being built at Kitimat, a few miles south of Prince Rupert. As a result of these developments there has been a great increase in shipping on the coast. Many of the channels
Canada Shipping Act
are dangerous, and ships are operating in weather in which they would not have operated a few years ago. The whole problem of the safety of ships on the west coast has become very important. I would ask the minister to tell the house about the present situation with regard to the use of radar on Canadian ships.

speechtext:
I should like to say a few words with regard to the amendments which are proposed to the Canada Shipping Act. I believe sincerely that any regulation or any amendment which will protect the travelling public should be supported by each and every member in the House of Commons. During the past few years there have been several tragedies on the inland waters of Canada which have brought a great deal of criticism so far as the Canada Shipping Act is concerned. The general public seems to feel that the regulations have not been enforced to the extent they should be. One other criticism one hears on many occasions is the fact that, in some cases, the regulations are enforced on small boats when the general public feels it is not necessary. Again I would say that any regulation which protects the travelling public should be supported.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) has mentioned the radiotelephone and radar. I would say that in the bay of Fundy region the radiotelephone is one of the greatest things that has ever come to the assistance of men who work on the water. As many hon. members know, I spent many years on the water myself. When you are out at night, miles away from any contact of any kind and with nothing but a diesel or gas engine to depend upon, you put in many anxious hours. Today, with radiotelephone equipment, you are in touch with your office or other boats every ten or fifteen minutes, and that removes a great deal

Canada Shipping Act
of the worry. You know that if anything happens someone can come to your assistance.
One other thing mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was radar equipment. Again* I want to agree wholeheartedly with what he has said. I should like to refer briefly to a ferry service in my county which plies between Deer island and L'Etete, which is on the mainland. This ferry service carries thousands of cars and tens of thousands of passengers annually. The distance is only about three miles, but it is through very dangerous waters. There are two narrow passages where the water flows very rapidly in both the flood tide and the ebb tide. There are ledges for the whole distance of three miles.
The men who operate that ferry, particularly in foggy weather, have an enormous responsibility. I do believe that radar equipment would tend to eliminate a lot of that, and would be a great protection to the public. I feel that in the not too distant future it may be necessary to insist that that type of equipment be installed on services of that nature to protect the general public. We have had one or two accidents on that ferry service, but without loss of life and without loss of property. They could have been serious. I do endorse the idea of radiotelephone equipment on any type of boat or ferry that is carrying passengers, particularly since the cost of that type of equipment is reasonable.
This bill will come before the committee. I am a member of the committee, and I am sure it will be interesting to have an opportunity to discuss the different amendments which are under consideration at this time. Before I take my seat, I want to emphasize the fact that anything we may do that will compel these operators to instal radiotelephone and radar equipment will be endorsed by the general public.

should like to say a few words on this bill, Mr. Speaker. I am not quite sure whether it applies to minor waters, but I do want to bring to the minister's attention a situation that exists in my constituency. From 1898 until about 1948 the passenger steamers that are operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and which gave very good service to that district during those years, were in the habit of carrying drums of gasoline on the bow of the steamer for delivery to small, isolated points where there is no other means of communication. I mention this because I see that a section in the bill deals with some exemption for steamships under five tons, yachts and tow barges.
(Mr. Stuart (Charlotte).]
I think in 1948, owing to a visit by an inspector of the Department of Transport or the maritime commission, these steamers were prohibited from carrying drums of gasoline on the bow for delivery to these isolated settlements. This proved a great hardship to many of these people. I know of people with good farms 20 to 30 miles away from any other settlement, who have to hire a tug and barge to get a few drums of gasoline in to operate their spray pumps, farm machinery and so on. At the present time the Canadian Pacific Railway also operates these passenger steamers on the Arrow and Kootenay lakes, to push railway car barges going to various points. Even under present circumstances they are prevented from putting a few drums of gasoline on the bow of the railway car barge being pushed by the steamer. This has proven a great hardship to many people living in isolated districts on the Arrow and Kootenay lakes.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister because I understand that they are allowed to carry empty gas drums on the steamers which, from my point of view, are much more hazardous as far as fire is concerned than are full drums of gasoline. I should like the minister and his officials to give consideration to the really unusual circumstances in which many of these communities have been placed because of this recent prohibition against the carrying of gasoline on the bows of passenger steamers or even on car barges being pushed by passenger steamers. I know of one community- its name is Johnsons Landing; the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) would know it quite well-where difficulty has arisen. Just recently I had a letter from farmers in that district who require gasoline for the operation of their spray pumps, their tractors and things of that sort, and who actually are obliged to hire a tug and a barge at a cost of $100 a* day in order to take into that small landing two or three dozen barrels of gasoline.
I mention this matter, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is a somewhat unusual circumstance. I cannot see any fire hazard in allowing these steamers to carry gasoline on their bows or on the bows of barges, as they did from 1898 until 1948.

However, I want to deal with the question which was raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Canada Shipping Act
Stuart), namely that in this bill there is no mention of radar.
It was stated that most ships have radar.
I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra himself gave the answer or the reason for the non-introduction of radar in this amendment. It is that radar is a new development. We know something about telephones and telegraph. In fact we know a great deal about telephones. We have them in operation every day. We operate them on ships. We operate them from ship to ship and from ship to shore, and they work well. We know the telephone is a sure factor. The same thing can be said about telegraphy. But the same thing cannot be said concerning radar. By that I do not mean that radar is not a good aid to navigation. I believe that it is; and we most certainly encourage all our government ships to have radar on them. But the position of radar is that it is not required by the safety of life at sea convention.
The safety of life at sea convention studied and considered the necessity of radar as an aid to navigation and have recommended against it. The last convention discussed the matter fully but did not make mandatory the installation of radar on ships. As I stated earlier, radar is but an aid to navigation and is not meant to replace the efficiency of the captain, the master or his mates, because the vessel is always in his charge. It is felt that the best we in the Department of Transport can do with reference to radar is to encourage the officers and the crew to receive training in radar. That we are doing at the moment for all new officers, and we make it a requirement for them in obtaining a certificate of proficiency. I think that answers the point which was raised.
May I say that during the course of last summer I remember an occasion when I was on a government ship trying to get into a port on the north shore of the river St. Lawrence when there was an extremely thick fog. In the radar we could see the bell which was anchored some distance from the wharf. We could see the wharf. We could hear people talking on the wharf but we could not get to it because at a certain stage in the course of the ship we went beyond the wharf and then it seemed that we were completely lost in so far as radar was concerned. We therefore had to go on our journey, anchor some distance from that wharf and go to it the next morning.
I realized then that while radar is an extremely important thing, and you can see ahead of you the whole river or the coast or the gulf, there are times when, if you get

Canada Shipping Act
off your course, it can be ineffective. Our thinking therefore has been that until the safety of life at sea convention and others who are experts in the field make it mandatory, we should not include it in the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act.

speechtext:
Last year, Mr. Chairman, before any discussion took place on the details of the estimates of the Department of Transport, I gave a short summary to the members of the committee on the affairs of the department, touching upon the major projects and explaining some of the increases which appear therein. If it meets with the approval of the committee, I would like to follow the same practice this year.
For 1953-54 the net total estimated expenditures for transport, including the air transport board, the board of transport commissioners, the Canadian maritime commission, and the national harbours board, amount to $118,256,000 as against $110,307,000 for the fiscal year 1952-53, or an increase of $7,949,000. For the Department of Transport proper the estimated expenditures for the coming fiscal year are stated at $105,365,000, or an increase of $4,747,000.
I would like to refer in this short statement to the Department of Transport only, and to review the estimates along the lines of the summary of standard objects of expenditures and special categories attached to the estimates book.
The first object is that which deals with civil salaries and wages. It is estimated that the department will need $975,000 more in this coming fiscal year than in the previous year, to cover the 11,351 positions on the establishment. This additional money requirement is brought about by such items as annual increases; basic salary rates increases; over-all increases for prevailing rate employees, etc.
However, I should like to call attention to the fact that some $300,000 of the increase is traceable to the need of providing 60 crew

members for the new icebreaker D'Iberville, which will come into operation early in 1953, and 22 additional positions to cover enlarged meteorological services for the Department of National Defence.
Despite the need for the 82 positions to which I have just referred, we have managed to pare our requirements to such an extent that we are providing for 191 positions less than in the fiscal year 1952-53. For the most part this substantial reduction was effected by electrification of certain aids to marine navigation, installation of more modern equipment on the older main-line canals and the leasing, for operation on a concession basis, of the Skyways Club hotel and the bakery at Gander, Newfoundland, which were formerly operated by the department with a staff of 143.
In short, the highlights of this object are the reduction in the number of positions covered in the estimates and the additional cost brought about by increases in the various rates of pay for employees in the department.
Object No. 4 is for professional and special services. The expected increase for the coming fiscal year amounts to $319,000. Of this sum, $210,000 is made necessary by expansion in investigation and planning for the St. Lawrence seaway, and $71,000 is due to increased rates of pay for lightkeeper assistants and for increased costs of operating three lightships by contract.
Possibly this would be a good place to pause for a moment to bring the committee up to date on the present position of the St. Lawrence seaway project. The committee will remember that in 1951, following the delays and the shelving to some extent by Congress of the 1941 agreement, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) went to Washington and discussed the project with the then president of the United States. It was then agreed that Canada and the United States would jointly make application to the international joint commission for approval of the power works in the international section, on condition that Canada would give its undertaking that it would build a seaway on the Canadian side of the international line.
The next step following that visit of the Prime Minister to the president of the United States was legislation brought down in this House of Commons. That legislation first of all established a St. Lawrence seaway authority providing for the building of the two canals, one at Lachine and one at the international section, and the locks of the Beauhaxnois canal, and the operation and maintenance of those canals.
The other piece of legislation was an agreement between Canada and Ontario by which
Supply-Transport
Ontario undertook to build and construct all works having to do with power. Following that legislation a joint application by the governments of Canada and the United States was made to the international joint commission. As the committee will recall, this commission sat in several places, both in Canada and the United States; and after sitting for less than five months brought down a decision approving of what is known as the 238/242 single stage control scheme. In other words, the international joint commission stated that the scheme was a feasible one from the engineering standpoint, and issued its order of approval.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: What date?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
I think that was in October, 1952; less than five months after the application was launched. There were certain conditions attached to the order, one being the removal of the Gut dam. As the house knows, the Gut dam was removed in a very short period of time, and I believe by early January there was nothing left.
The next step was an application by the New York state power authority to the federal power commission of the United States for a licence to develop power in the international section jointly with an entity to be named by Canada. Of course the entity named by Canada in the legislation is the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission. That application is still pending. Evidence has been heard by the examiner, and at the last hearing which took place late last month the examiner had to deal with the applications of New York and another applicant. What his report will be to the federal power commission I am not in position to state because it has not been made public, but that is where the matter stands.
Two things still require to be done before we can go ahead with the power development. The first is the granting of the licence to the present applicant, the New York state power authority, and the naming of the entity, which I presume would be the licensee, by the government of the United States. The moment those two things are done the project can proceed immediately.
Meanwhile a series of bills have been placed before Congress for consideration. One by Senator Wiley would seek to develop jointly with Canada the navigational features of the project, and takes for granted that the power commission will grant a licence to the New York state power authority. The other bill is by Senator Lehman and has to do with both power and navigation. It also concerns the division of responsibility for power as

Supply-Transport
between the state and the federal government. In effect that is where the matter rests today.
Our hope is that the federal power commission will grant a licence to the New York state power authority and that the administration at Washington will name the licensee as the entity. The moment that is done we can proceed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: That is with the power plan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
We can proceed with the power development. It follows that not very long after we must proceed with the navigational features of the project.
Object No. 5 deals with travelling, transportation and removal expenses and shows an over-all increase of $4,800. The civil estimates of the department for 1953-54 under this object actually show a decrease of $8,900, but this is offset by the Department of National Defence item recoverable of $13,600 under their meteorological services.
Object No. 6 covers freight, express and cartage and shows a net increase of $18,900. As in the previous item of travelling expenses, the department proper will be able to get along with less money but a national defence department requirement of $22,800 in meteorological services will more than balance our decrease.
Object No. 8 covers telephone, telegrams and other communication services. There is an increase here of $205,900 over last year's requirements. The main reason is the expansion of meteorological services, both civil and for national defence.
Object No. 12 deals with materials and supplies. Here we have been obliged to allow for an increase of $372,400. Primarily the increased requirement under this object results from the need of providing $260,000 to cover the first year's operation of the new icebreaker D'Iberville.
While I am on this object I should like to mention that the leasing of the Skyways hotel and bakery at Gander, Newfoundland enables the department to show a decrease in materials and supplies requirements of some $220,400. Hon. members will agree that this is a step in the right direction, as I see no need for the Department of Transport to operate facilities which can be leased on a concession basis to private enterprise.
Object No. 13, covering construction or acquisition of buildings and works, including land, constitutes the second largest item of expenditure in the Department of Transport for the fiscal year 1953-54. There are 15 votes included, 8 of which show decreases

totalling $2,600,000 and 7 votes with increases of $6,300,000, making a net increase in this object of $3,700,000.
I would like to review briefly some of the projects that come under this object. In canals, for instance, there is a reduction of $1,400,000, brought about because we have completed the St. Remi tunnel under the Lachine canal. We have an item in here for the building of the Atwater tunnel. The estimated cost of this new tunnel, under the Lachine canal which was undertaken to alleviate traffic conditions on one of the main arteries of Montreal, is $6,500,000. Hon. members will remember that there were two suggested tunnels to be undertaken by the department, the first one, which I mentioned earlier, being the St. Remi tunnel. By virtue of an agreement made between the city of Montreal and the Department of Transport, the city is contributing one-third of the cost up to $4,500,000 for St. Remi and $6 million in the case of the Atwater tunnel. The estimated gross expenditure to the end of the present fiscal year at Atwater is $4,700,000, and the balance of $1,800,000 is now being provided.
The next largest item is to provide proper facilities in the Laredo channel on the west coast of British Columbia for shipping services at Kitimat. This channel has been chosen as the best route for ocean-going vessels entering and leaving the terminals of the Alcan development. After several meetings held with shipping and pilotage interests, it was decided that one major light station and fog alarm would be required. I need not go on to deal in detail with what is being done, as I cam go into that later. The main point I wish to make is that we have decided to provide proper navigational facilities to assist in the development at Kitimat.
In the appropriation for the river St. Lawrence ship channel, contract dredging, we have included an annual amount called for by the contract, namely $2,500,000. This is a five-year contract which was awarded in 1952 to Marine Industries Limited after calling for tenders, and calls for an over-all expenditure of $13,022,000. The amount being provided in this year's estimates represents a decrease of $300,000.
By far the largest item under construction of buildings and works in the Department of Transport for this coming fiscal year is that associated with continuation of the crossing of the strait of Canso involving the construction of a causeway with a lock on the Cape Breton side to allow navigation through the strait. Last year parliament voted the sum of $2,250,000. This year we are asking for $6,700,000, or an increase of $4,450,000.

Hon. members will recall that on May 16, 1952, I announced that a contract for the rock fill required in the causeway had been let to the Northern Construction Company and J. W. Stewart Limited for $5,786,000. It is estimated that by March 31, 1953, $1,300,000 will have been spent on the causeway proper, and we are making provision for $3 million to cover this phase of the work.
An amount of $2 million is included here for the navigation lock at the northern end of the causeway, and the house will remember that this afternoon, prior to orders of the day, I announced that the contract for the lock had been awarded to T. C. Gorman (Nova Scotia) Limited of Halifax at $4,800,000 odd.
The Canadian National Railways is expected to initiate the relocation of its railway trackage in connection with the causeway during the coming fiscal year, and we are providing $1,450,000 to cover the cost of that work. I am happy to say that the contract for the rock fill with the Northern Construction Company is progressing very satisfactorily. Over 1,000 feet of the causeway had already been constructed to the end of January, and reports which I have from the firm of consulting engineers who are supervising the Canso project, O. J. McCulloch and Company, indicate that no delay is foreseen in the completion of the project in late 1955.
I should like to refer now to some of the contracts having to do with transportation services between Newfoundland and the mainland. At North Sydney the construction of new terminals, which began in late 1949, is progressing in a satisfactory manner. The contractor on this project is T. C. Gorman (Nova Scotia) Limited of Halifax who completed the dredging necessary for construction of the dock. In the coming year we expect that the new North Sydney terminals will be completed, and we are providing for an expenditure of $599,000 to cover the transit shed, elevators on the dock, railway trackage, roadway paving and the construction of an office and waiting room and a parking lot. The total cost of the new terminals when completed will be in excess of $2,900,000. The amount required for the present fiscal year is smaller than that for the previous one by $581,000.
The Port aux Basques terminals will cost the federal government $4,400,000 over and above the expenditure to be made by the Canadian National Railways at that point. The estimated expenditure to the end of the fiscal year 1952-53 is slightly less than $2 million, and during the coming fiscal year we are anticipating an expenditure of $2,-
300,000	with the work to be finalized in the
Supply-Transport
late spring of 1954. The main contract for the construction and excavation was let to McNamara Construction Company of Toronto, and tenders are to be called shortly for the foundation and erection of the transit shed on the dock itself. The contract for the design and manufacture of two 25-ton capacity marine elevators was let to Colby Crane and Engineering Company of Vancouver at a cost of $220,000. The design and supervision of the dock and transit shed is under contract with O. J. McCulloch and Company, consulting engineers of Montreal. In addition to construction of the terminal facilities at North Sydney and Port aux Basques, there is the construction of the auto ferry vessel, and I shall deal with this vessel in my subsequent remarks on object No. 16, construction or acquisition of equipment.
I turn now for a moment to expenditures having to do with the air services branch of the department and which reflect the expansion of air navigation throughout the country.
I shall treat first with the civil aviation division. Although the total outlay for that division is especially large-the exact amount is $8,465,500-it is difficult to explain the item in anything more than a very general manner. The reason for this lies in the fact that the component parts are characterized by their number rather than by their size. For instance, there is $2,800,000 provided for new runways or extensions at ten locations such as Charlottetown, Forestville, Timmins, Regina, Prince Rupert. There is $1,085,000 for strengthening and resurfacing of runways and clearing approaches at several airports.
There is approximately $1J million covering installation or improvements of lighting at 39 airfields. There are 21 projects for water, sewer, steam lines, etc. There are 40 projects having to do with the construction of power plants, living accommodation, garages, workshops, hangars, stores buildings and the like. Nevertheless there are a few major undertakings which go to make up substantial parts of the $8J million. Those which I have in mind are:
Dartmouth, $850,000 for reinforcing and lengthening one runway to accommodate heavier aircraft.
Gander, $750,000 for rehabilitation of runway and taxi strip.
Grande Prairie, $500,000 for runway reconstruction.
Regina, $500,000 for construction of a new runway.
Saskatoon, $400,000 for construction of terminal building.
Timmins, $375,000 for construction of one runway. This field will eventually replace Porquis.

Supply-Transport
Forestville, $300,000 for extension and paving of runway to accommodate heavier aircraft.
Rouyn, $300,000 for the same purpose as at Forestville.
Prince George, $210,000 for reconstruction of taxi strip and turning button.
Gander, $200,000 to cover first stage of renovation of terminal building.
Our radio aviation services financial requirements for capital construction and acquisition total $2,100,000 and relate to all radio facilities necessary for operation of the airways system, such as radio range stations, beacons, communication facilities, radio installation for instrument landing systems, and associated dwellings and the like.
The telegraph and telephone services contemplate expenditures aggregating $900,000 in connection with the reconstruction and expansion of their existing facilities. There are two large projects involved: (1) installation of a radio relay system between Ashcroft and Prince George, British Columbia, which will be capable of handling a large number of commercial long distance telephone circuits, for which $300,000 is included, and (2) installation of carrier and repeater equipment in the interior of British Columbia, at a cost of $100,000.
I think I could finish in about five minutes, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Go ahead.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Under object No. 16, which has to do with construction or acquisition of equipment, it will be seen from the title of this classification that there must necessarily be a very substantial annual expenditure by the Department of Transport because it comprises numerous operating units entirely distinct one from the other. A glance at the summary will show that we are proposing a total expenditure of $10,081,000, and that this represents a cut-back of approximately $1J million from last year's figure. I should like to deal with these seriatim.
Topping the list under this object is an amount of $6,368,000 which is included in vote 472, construction of auto ferry vessels, and covers the anticipated expenditures during 1953-54 in respect of the North Sydney-Port aux Basques vessel and the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor vessel.
As to the North Sydney-Port aux Basques vessel, the committee will recall that by virtue of the terms of union between Canada and Newfoundland in 1949 the government undertook to provide a ferry service capable of handling motor vehicle traffic between North Sydney and Port aux Basques as soon as the

highway was completed in Newfoundland. I understand that a through highway between St. John's and Port aux Basques will not be available until 1956; nevertheless we have gone ahead with the improvement already mentioned for new terminals at North Sydney and Port aux Basques, and at the same time parliament last year approved money to be expended on the construction of a new automobile ferry vessel. The construction of the vessel, together with the preparation of detailed plans and specifications, was allocated to Canadian Vickers Limited of Montreal on February 17, 1951.
I have already given on a number of occasions details of the construction of this specialized unit, and I thought I would simply say that it is the feeling of the government and of the Canadian National Railways, who will be entrusted with the operation of the new ferry vessel, that it is expected this ship, together with the new terminals, will bring tremendous improvement in the transportation service to Newfoundland and will for the first time make it possible for motor vehicle traffic to be carried across Cabot strait.
It is true that the ship as now designed will not carry a large number of trucks or trailers, but one must bear in mind that until such time as a clear indication is given of the type of traffic which will be moved by truck, it is well-nigh impossible to design a vessel which could be operated economically and, at the same time, provide a year round service for the bulk of the traffic which is handled by the Canadian National between the two points.
My officers have gone into the question of the movement of refrigerated fish traffic and advise me that it is very doubtful that fresh fish from Newfoundland could move by truck to market. The research and development department of the Canadian National is now working on a method of handling fresh fish which might very well revolutionize the fishing industry in Newfoundland and in the maritimes. This new method is still in the process of being developed in co-operation with the fisheries council of Canada. Furthermore, I am informed that the movement of heavy tractors and trailers in the province of Nova Scotia is very much restricted by the size and condition of highway bridges.
I must repeat again that it is a specialized construction, and numerous problems have lo be ironed out from time to time between ihe naval architects, the shipyard, manufacturers, etc. The target date has been reviewed recently, and I am advised that the ship will be ready to enter into service in the summer of 1954. The estimated cost is $7,500,000;

$2,200,000 has already been spent, and provision is made in this year's estimates for $5,368,000.
The second car ferry is to operate between Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, and Bar Harbor, Maine. Tenders were called last fall and the shipyard which has received the contract for its construction is Davie Shipbuilding and Repairing Company Limited of Lauzon, Quebec.
This ferry vessel is also a specialized unit, since it must carry passenger automobiles and trucks as well as provide accommodation for the handling of a large number of passengers. The service speed of the vessel has been set at 18J knots, in order to allow her to make a round trip every day between the two terminals. This is an important feature in the operation of the vessel in order that it may, we hope, be operated without the provision of a subsidy. We must obtain the greatest utilization possible from this unit, hence the necessity for its high speed.
I have already given to the house the details of the construction of this ship, but I want to add that we are providing for the expenditure of $1,000,000 in the 1953-54 estimates.
The next largest amount to which I draw attention is the sum of $1,200,000 provided in vote 452, steamers construction. This particular sum is $4 million less than we were obliged to expend last year, and such reduction is traceable to the fact that, whereas last year approximately $4,300,000 was needed for the new icebreaker D'Iberville, an amount of $300,000 only, being the final payment, is now required. The appropriation to which I have referred just now also includes $750,000 for the lighthouse supply and buoy vessel which will operate out of Saint John, New Brunswick. The estimated cost of this vessel is $2,225,000. It is expected to call for tenders for this vessel in June of this year.
A further $100,000 is being provided to cover the first stage of construction on a lighthouse supply and buoy vessel for the agency at Victoria, British Columbia, which will cost approximately $1,125,000. This latter vessel is urgently needed. The two vessels now used in the agency in maintaining the navigational aids are both very old and are proving quite inadequate.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to impose any longer on the patience of the house. I have covered, in a general way, the main votes
Supply-Transport
that will be brought forward for consideration of the committee, and I am sure that with this general statement all members will be in a far better position to discuss the estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Can the minister tell us when we may expect the annual report for his department for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1952? It may have been issued, but I have been unable to get a copy and I understand that it is not yet available for distribution.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: No, it is not, and unfortunately I cannot give an exact date. I do know that there is always some delay in that report because it is a pretty comprehensive one. Perhaps tomorrow I will be able to tell my hon. friend just exactly when we can have it for him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question or two? I did not hear the amount that was in the estimates for the new boat to be built for the Wood island-Caribou service. There was a lot of conversation going on behind me, and I did not get just what amount was included for the new runway extension at Charlottetown.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
The answer to the first question is that the decision to build the Northumberland ship was not arrived at until after the main estimates had been tabled. It is not covered in the main estimates, and it will be included in the supplementary estimates.
The answer to the second question is that we have determined to spend an amount to extend the runway at Charlottetown provided the city will undertake to operate and maintain the airport. I do not know where that stands, but my recollection is that the municipality is willing to do that. There will be an item, but I cannot give the amount.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext: Tomorrow we shall resume the debate on the budget, and I am so hopeful that we shall conclude that debate that I will announce that we shall take up the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration afterward.
